item.title: The Gut-Brain-Libido Axis
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

The Gut-Brain-Libido Axis

Do gut microbes hold the key to a better sex life?

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Gut microbes can affect your mood and sociability via the gut-brain axis.
  • Gut microbes also recycle hormones, moderating your libido.
  • A compromised gut lining can lead to system inflammation, turning off the sex drive.

"Science is like sex: sometimes something useful comes out, but that is not the reason we are doing it." —Richard Feynman

We tend to think of ourselves as philosophical creatures, but from an evolutionary perspective, we are basically gonads with supporting organs. Thus, seven billion people swarm the Earth. As Darwin might have said, it’s all about the sex.

Source: jackphoto / iStock

Surprisingly, animals need microbial facilitators in their sexual conquest. We may think we own the planet, but we are transient interlopers in a largely microbial world. Since most of these tiny creatures perceive us as lunch, we need to protect ourselves. That is the job of our immune system, but for all of its marvelous ability to adapt to new threats, microbes can run circles around our fortifications.

That is why, millennia ago, we recruited our own microbes to act as our first line of defense. It takes a microbe to fight a microbe.

In return for a continuous feast and a warm spot to reproduce, our homegrown microbes dutifully stab, poison, starve, or eat pathogens who foolishly enter our shared lair. A well-curated collection of microbes, called the microbiome, can spell the difference between good health and bad.

The Body Under Stress

Our body has a tripwire that snaps under stress, causing us to switch to panic mode. It gathers all our energy to fight or flee a potential threat. It draws that energy from other bodily systems, including the immune system. It also pulls from the libido, the name Freud gave to the sex drive. When you are running from a tiger, there’s no time for lust.

For those beset by demanding bosses or an unjust world, the stress puts a real damper on our love lives. This stress likely plays a role in our declining birth rates.

But our microbiome also plays a role. When it gets unbalanced (called dysbiosis), it can create a stress of its own, pretty much indistinguishable from external stress.

The microbiome can pull other strings as well. Our sex hormones, headlined by testosterone and estrogen, have a strange relationship to gut microbes. Once in circulation, hormones need to be controlled, or they can drive us mad. That job falls partly to the liver, which places hormones into molecular cages made of sugars and proteins in a process called conjugation. Thus packaged and inactivated, the liver slips the hormones into bile, which it sends to the digestive system for excretion.

But certain microbes in our gut like to snack on these cages, liberating the hormones. That’s how microbes act as a source of human sex hormones. A healthy microbiome produces optimal hormone levels, while a dysbiotic microbiome disrupts the hormonal balance, leading to a loss of libido.

The Gut-Brain Axis

article continues after advertisement

Research by John Cryan, Ted Dinan, and others has shown that microbes can affect our sex drive via the gut-brain axis in various other ways.

On the negative side, some microbes produce toxins that induce anxiety and depression. This can be exacerbated by a leaky gut. Systemic inflammation can impair blood flow and dampen the brain circuits involved in arousal and sexual performance.

On the positive side, beneficial gut microbes can produce neurotransmitters—the chemicals that nerve cells use to communicate—including serotonin and dopamine, which are the targets of antidepressants. These neurotransmitters may communicate with our brain via cells in the gut called neuropods.

Depressed people are not, in general, thinking about sex. In fact, a core feature of depression is anhedonia: an absence of enjoyment, interest, and sexual motivation.

Cryan and Dinan have shown that certain microbes can improve anhedonia and mood in general. They coined the term psychobiotic to refer to these microbes as well as the prebiotic foods they like. By tweaking stress levels, sex hormones, and neurotransmitters, microbes play an outsized role in erectile dysfunction and libido.

If the thought of trillions of tiny microbes controlling your sex life gives you goosebumps, take heart. You may not have much control over your stressful environment, but you have an amazing leverage over your gut microbes.

You’re in Charge of Your Gut

According to a recent review by Italian researchers Giuseppe Marano, Marianna Mazza, and colleagues, “Lifestyle factors, including diet, stress, and antibiotic use, can modulate the gut microbiota and, consequently, sexual health outcomes.”

article continues after advertisement

You can tip the balance of your gut microbes to be healthier and sexier with some specific changes. These are not shocking interventions: exercise more, sleep better, and eat your veggies.

The veggies with the greatest impact are the ones with fiber and polyphenols, which are the preferred food for psychobiotic gut microbes. These include colorful foods like beets and berries, as well as fibrous foods like lentils, artichokes, onions, and beans.

There are important caveats here. These foods are potent, and if you are accustomed to a lot of processed food, you may be in for a shock. Start slowly, or you may get gassy and bloated, something that makes a lot of people jump ship prematurely. Also, if you are having a flare-up of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), wait for symptoms to resolve, or you could exacerbate the situation. Talk to your doctor about diet changes if you have intestinal issues.

Boosting your good microbes can make you feel better and boost your libido. Once you get sexier, you’ll want everyone else to be sexier too, so pass this post around.

item.title: Pleasers and Pleaders
item.description:
People-Pleasing

Pleasers and Pleaders

The people-pleaser is half of a dance. The other half almost never gets named.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Pleasers and pleaders usually grew up learning the same thing: Asking for what you want directly isn’t safe.
  • Across two studies, healthy selfishness was a strong positive predictor of well-being and self-esteem.
  • Pathological altruism was the single strongest predictor of depression.
Source: timsa/Getty Images

Most relationship advice treats the people pleaser as a problem to be solved. There are books, podcasts, Instagram carousels— heck, entire wellness industries— built around helping the pleaser say no. And don’t get me wrong, chronic people pleasers often are desperate for help, and there is help out there for them (I wrote a chapter about this in Rise Above). But here is what every one of those well-meaning resources misses: The people-pleaser is half of a dance. The other half — the pleader — almost never gets named. I think that’s a pretty important part of the equation.

I call this person the “pleader” to make clear that these folks aren’t necessarily “toxic." The pleader is simply someone who asks again and again and again after you’ve already said “no thanks." The pleader is someone who may acknowledge your boundary in one sentence, only to completely undo it in the next breath.

But I want to be clear: The pleader isn’t the villain in this story. Pleasers and pleaders usually grew up learning the same thing: Asking for what you want directly isn't safe. Pleasers dealt with that by giving and never asking for anything back, whereas pleaders found sneakier ways to get what they need.

I’ve spent the last decade studying the personality structure of what I’m calling the pleader side. With my colleagues Brandon Weiss, Joshua Miller, and Keith Campbell, I’ve published on the clinical correlates of vulnerable narcissism. The defining features of vulnerable narcissism are shame, entitlement, distrust of others, and extreme sensitivity to perceived slights. The “entitlement paradox” I write about in Rise Above is “I’m broken and I am entitled to special treatment because I’m broken.”

So how do pleaders get what they want? They show you how fragile they are (and they often are truly fragile), how hard things have been, and how much they’re hurting. They let their distress do the talking, and they make your “no” the reason they’re in pain.

Typical Patterns of a Pleader

Pleasers give too much, and pleaders ask too much. You may recognize these pleader patterns:

  1. Getting other people on their side. Pleaders will call your other friends to get them on their side before they even bring up the disagreement with you. And once the fight starts, they bring in reinforcements: “Your sister agrees with me.” “Even my therapist thinks so.”
  2. Being dramatic. "I do everything around here." Pleaders say it with such certainty, like it's just a fact. The pleader is a master at picking words that make you feel guilty for not giving them the constant attention they crave.
  3. Turning what they didn’t do into a favor. The pleader forgets to call when they said they would, then tells you, “Oh, I didn’t want to overwhelm you.”
  4. Saying it’s “just an opinion,” then pushing you anyway. “I’m not telling you what to do, but… you look terrible in that beard and should cut it off.” They say it all warmly, like they’re just offering an opinion. But in the same breath, they’re telling you to do the exact thing they just said you didn’t have to do.
  5. Going after your sore spot. Pleasers are obsessed with the question, “Am I a kind person?”—and pleaders sure do know it. So they will say things like, “I just wish you cared more,” or “You’re so cold sometimes,” softly, often with a hurt look. And you know what? It works like a charm on pleasers.
article continues after advertisement

Pleaders don’t have to be doing any of this on purpose, and often they aren’t. Pleaders aren’t necessarily psychopaths, or narcissists, or toxic. Pleaders are people whose survival strategy is doing what every survival strategy does: running in the background, beneath the level of conscious choice.

How Does the Dance Get Going?

Pleaders and pleasers often find each other without anyone introducing them. They are like birds of a feather, except in this case it’s wounds of a feather. The pleader’s antennae are calibrated for someone who won’t say no cleanly. The pleaser’s antennae are calibrated for someone who needs them.

In fact, pleasers and pleaders often come from the very same family. A controlling parent who needs everyone to stay tuned in to their feelings at all times can raise kids who end up as pleasers, pleaders, or a mix of both. A lot of pleasers grow up giving before anyone asks, desperately trying to figure out what everyone needs just to keep things calm.

Pleaders usually got punished for asking for things directly, so they learned to show how much they were hurting instead.

What’s the Way Out for Both Parties?

Most advice is written for the pleaser. Trust your radar. Say no. All true. But the pleaser cannot do this work alone, because it takes two to tango.

For the pleaser: Learn to trust your own radar without checking it with someone else first. The pleaser’s wound is uncertainty about whether their perception is fair. The work is letting accuracy be enough.

The deeper work, the one I’ve spent a lot of time measuring, is healthy selfishness. My colleague Emanuel Jauk and I built a scale that captures it (take the test here). My healthy selfishness scale has items like: “I have healthy boundaries,” and “I give myself permission to enjoy myself, even if it doesn’t necessarily help others.” On the other end, we have pathological altruism, which is chronic over-giving that people often don’t even want.

Across two studies, healthy selfishness was a strong positive predictor of well-being, life satisfaction, and self-esteem, whereas pathological altruism was the single strongest predictor of depression. And the childhood antecedent that most predicted high pathological altruism in our adult samples? You got it: “As a child, I was often encouraged by my family to substitute my own needs for their own.”

article continues after advertisement

The work for the pleaser, then, isn’t to give less. It’s to give from a self that hasn’t been substituted out of the room.

For the pleader: Learn to ask directly, without leverage. When someone tells you no, take it as their final answer. Your suffering can be completely real, and it still doesn’t mean anyone owes you something. Deep down, pleaders aren’t sure anyone will say yes when they ask directly. In a healthy relationship, they’ll find out that people do.

For both pleasers and pleaders: The healthiest relationship is one where both people have stopped playing their old roles. But in a healthy, growth-oriented relationship, people ask for what they want directly, get straight answers, and walk away still feeling like themselves.

I think that’s what we’re all really looking for, even when we’re doing the old dance.

item.title: The Washington University Approach to Psychopathology
item.description:
Psychiatry

The Washington University Approach to Psychopathology

What the WashU school can teach us about psychiatric classification.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • The Washington University school developed a scientific approach to psychiatric diagnosis.
  • Robins and Guze proposed five phases for establishing the validity of psychiatric diagnoses in 1970.
  • DSM-III improved diagnostic reliability but departed from the WashU group's emphasis on validity.
Brookings Hall, Washington University in St. Louis.
Source: Endersan / Used with permission

As the American Psychiatric Association moves toward the next edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), questions concerning psychiatric diagnosis and classification will once again come to the forefront. Surprisingly, relatively little has been written for general audiences about one of the most important developments in the history of psychiatric diagnosis: the Washington University approach to psychopathology.

Developed at Washington University in St. Louis during the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s, this approach sought to establish psychiatry firmly as a branch of medicine by grounding psychiatric diagnosis in empirical research rather than theoretical speculation or professional consensus. Its influence was enormous, although many of its central principles were eventually neglected.

I wish here to briefly describe this approach, which informs my recent proposal with psychiatrist Ronald W. Pies for a validity-based diagnostic hierarchy in DSM-6, forthcoming in Psychiatric Services.

The Historical Background

In the mid-20th century, American psychiatry was dominated by psychoanalysis, which generally placed little emphasis on formal diagnosis. With some notable exceptions, such as Roy R. Grinker Sr. and Otto Kernberg, psychoanalysts tended to classify patients broadly as either neurotic or psychotic, while the question of whether particular syndromes represented distinct diseases or conditions received less attention.

Psychiatry also faced criticism over diagnostic unreliability. David Rosenhan's influential 1973 study, although later discredited (Cahalan, 2019), fueled public skepticism. More compellingly, the U.S.–U.K. Diagnostic Project found that American psychiatrists diagnosed schizophrenia at roughly twice the rate of their British counterparts (Kendell et al., 1971), largely because of differences in diagnostic practice. Psychiatry needed more reliable diagnoses, but reliability alone would not establish whether those diagnoses represented actual conditions.

It was against this backdrop that a group of psychiatrists at Washington University in St. Louis, most notably Eli Robins, Samuel Guze, and George Winokur, developed a fundamentally different approach to psychiatric diagnosis.

The Problem of Psychiatric Classification

Unlike other branches of medicine, psychiatry generally lacks laboratory tests capable of establishing specific diagnoses. The 19th-century anatomical-clinical method linked symptoms to identifiable pathological changes, transforming much of medicine. In psychiatry, however, this method produced relatively few successes, apart from conditions such as neurosyphilis.

article continues after advertisement

The German psychiatrist Emil Kraepelin recognized that symptoms alone could not provide an adequate basis for classification. Many medical diseases produce fever, cough, fatigue, or pain; no one would seriously propose classifying diseases solely on the basis of such symptoms. The same principle applies to psychiatry: Similar symptoms may arise from fundamentally different diseases, while the same disease may present differently across patients or stages of illness. This is a point overlooked by contemporary dimensional and network approaches to psychopathology, which tend to treat symptoms as the primary data of psychiatry.

Kraepelin emphasized another source of evidence: the longitudinal course and outcome of illness. Dementia praecox (later renamed schizophrenia), manic-depressive insanity, and Alzheimer's disease could all involve psychotic symptoms, but their characteristic courses differed. Dementia praecox was chronic or deteriorating; manic-depressive illness was episodic and relapsing; Alzheimer's disease involved progressive cognitive deterioration, ultimately ending in death. By considering the course and outcome of illness, in addition to symptoms, Kraepelin discovered three diseases.

This basic insight remains essential to psychiatric classification. As Goodwin and Guze (1989) later emphasized, "Diagnosis is prognosis." A valid diagnosis should convey something meaningful about the nature and expected course of an illness, not merely describe its presenting symptoms.

The Washington University Approach

In 1970, Robins and Guze published their landmark paper, "Establishment of Diagnostic Validity in Psychiatric Illness: Its Application to Schizophrenia." They proposed that diagnoses be validated through convergence across multiple independent lines of evidence.

Their framework identified five phases: clinical description, laboratory studies, delimitation from other disorders, follow-up studies, and family studies. Clinical description establishes a syndrome's characteristic presentation; laboratory studies seek distinguishing findings; delimitation examines its boundaries with other conditions; follow-up studies assess course and outcome; and family studies investigate genetics and patterns of familial aggregation. Later researchers added other validators, including differential treatment response.

A crucial distinction here is between reliability and validity. A group of clinicians may agree on the criteria for a disorder without establishing that it represents a distinct disease. Nor does the frequent co-occurrence of symptoms establish an independent disease. Diagnostic validity instead depends on the convergence of evidence showing that a condition can be meaningfully distinguished from others.

article continues after advertisement

No single validator is necessarily decisive. Two diseases may share symptoms, genetic markers, or treatment responses while differing in course and other characteristics. Conversely, differences in symptoms do not necessarily establish separate diseases. The objective is to identify distinguishable forms of psychopathology, not simply to achieve diagnostic agreement.

From WashU to DSM-III

The Washington University school influenced Robert Spitzer, who led the development of DSM-III. The Feighner criteria (Feighner et al., 1972) and the subsequent Research Diagnostic Criteria (Spitzer et al., 1978) represented major advances in psychiatric classification, providing explicit criteria that different clinicians could apply consistently. Both projects substantially improved diagnostic reliability. In some ways, this was a major advance: clinical communication and research require agreement about what is being studied. A problem arises, however, when reliably defined categories are mistaken for validated diseases.

DSM-III, published in 1980, built on these advances but prioritized operational definitions and diagnostic reliability over the rigorous validation envisioned by Robins and Guze. Political compromises further shaped the classification, prompting several Washington University psychiatrists to resign from the DSM-III Task Force (Decker, 2013). Although DSM-III substantially improved psychiatric communication and research, it also introduced numerous diagnostic categories that lacked comparable evidence of validity.

How Many Psychiatric Conditions Are There?

The Feighner criteria paper initially described 14 psychiatric conditions, and the Research Diagnostic Criteria expanded this number to 25. In their 1989 textbook Psychiatric Diagnosis, Goodwin and Guze discussed roughly a dozen major syndromes for which they considered the validating evidence strong. Yet DSM-III had already included 265 diagnostic categories.

article continues after advertisement

Applying strict standards of diagnostic validity would require reconsidering many familiar DSM categories. Although a detailed examination is beyond the scope of this article, numerous widely accepted psychiatric diagnoses—including ADHD, most personality disorders, the dissociative disorders, and several depressive and anxiety disorders—would fail to meet conventional standards for validity as independent disease entities (Ghaemi et al., 2022).

Proliferating categories also create the appearance of extensive psychiatric comorbidity. A patient with one underlying condition may acquire several overlapping diagnoses, each describing a different manifestation of the same psychopathology. A classification intended to identify diseases can thus become an inventory of symptoms and syndromes without adequately establishing their distinctiveness.

A Proposal for DSM-6

In our forthcoming paper in Psychiatric Services, Pies and I propose a validity-based diagnostic hierarchy for DSM-6 (Ruffalo & Pies, in press). Diagnoses would be organized according to the strength of evidence supporting them, distinguishing well-validated syndromes from provisional or less-established constructs. Clinicians could continue to describe symptoms and clinically useful patterns without treating every descriptive category as an equally valid disease entity.

This does not mean that dimensional measurement has no place in psychiatry. Dimensions can be useful for assessing severity and describing variations within and across psychiatric syndromes. But they cannot, by themselves, establish whether particular diagnoses represent distinct conditions. That requires the kind of systematic investigation and convergence of evidence that Guze (1970) described as a commitment to "tough-mindedness."

As psychiatry prepares for DSM-6, it would do well to recover this approach. The central task of psychiatric classification is not simply to improve diagnostic agreement or develop increasingly elaborate descriptions of psychopathology, but to determine which conditions actually exist and how they differ from one another. This was the central concern of the Washington University group more than half a century ago, and it remains no less important today.

item.title: What Kind of Mom Might I Have Been?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

What Kind of Mom Might I Have Been?

Personal Perspective: A now-childfree-elder's take on what didn't happen.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • It's interesting to consider paths not taken in our lives.
  • Feelings about motherhood can shift over a lifetime without making a childfree life incomplete.
  • Developing a coherent life narrative, regardless of our specific circumstances, can be valuable.
Source: Jordyn St. John/Unsplash

“Mom, what would you have done if you didn’t have children?” I posed this question to my mother when in my early 50s, she in her 70s. What followed was my favorite conversation we ever had in our lifelong tense relationship.

She didn’t miss a beat, saying she’d have gotten a PhD. in English Literature in hopes of becoming a university professor. “That doesn’t mean I didn’t want you or your sisters,” she quickly added.

I liked that she could so easily envision a life without being a mother and told her so. In her moment of candor, she showed me a side of her character I’d never seen. I felt a tinge of acceptance as her only offspring who didn’t have kids and savored the undertone of regret I heard in her voice. She would have been a stern but dedicated educator.

What kind of mother might I have been had I had kids, I wonder?

I was well-prepared to care for an infant, having lots of experience with my sisters four to 10 years younger and the neighborhood kids I babysat regularly. Poopy diapers didn’t faze me, and only once did I get showered when changing a baby boy. I could burp them, cuddle them, and lure them to sleep at bedtime.

I liked playing with the older kids and helping them with their homework. When they cried over something that happened at school, I comforted them and, if asked, offered suggestions.

I did not excel at resolving sibling spats, more often leaving them to figure out their own repair processes. In hindsight, perhaps that was a clever strategy, but at the time I just wanted to remove myself from the fray. I confess, I did lose my cool periodically, too.

Always a frugal person, I would surely have chafed at the never-ending expenditures involved in childrearing. Had my ex and I been successful at getting pregnant, we would have become parents during a years-long period when he was unemployed. Who knows if one or two littles would have goaded him into a more fervent job hunt.

Source: Vesnazajchenko/Pixabay

I, on the other hand, was on an upward trajectory in my career and ambitious as a prize fighter for the belt. The man I married was the youngest in his family and had never changed a diaper. He was afraid of babies and perplexed by the raucous nature of most children.

My role at work would have partnered poorly with what surely would have been a home life with me as mom managing almost everything, all the time. I suspect our union would have ended 20 years before it did, and I would have raised the kids largely on my own. I cannot envision that scenario for more than a few minutes without a sense of doom for the kids I didn’t have.

article continues after advertisement

Managing my insecure, anxious temperament has involved lots of therapy and exercise over the years. I cannot conceive how working mothers, especially those who are single, manage the workload and expense involved in raising kids. I know many parents are physically active, but for the life of me, I can’t picture how they do it.

Of course, this is all pure conjecture, and I’ll never know how life may have unfolded differently than my reflections. What is sure, though, is that my feelings about becoming a mother have shifted throughout my life. I am whole as I am, thanks to therapy and a ton of hard work. I continue to integrate my life experiences into the coherent narrative of my life.

Today, I derive great joy from my many friendships with people younger than I, especially those born several decades after me. Many have kids; some don’t. I identify more with the non-parents, of course, whether they consider themselves childfree or childless. I appreciate the travails and delights of the moms and dads before they run off to whatever obligations soon beckon. I am grateful for whatever time they can share.

It struck me this morning while walking in the forest that the only person in the throughline of the story of my life is, and always will be, me. Although perhaps I’ll live on through the lives I have touched in ways I’ll never know. And that’s all good by me.

item.title: The Importance of Knowing Your Partner’s Attachment Style
item.description:
Attachment

The Importance of Knowing Your Partner’s Attachment Style

Exploring attachment styles can prevent misattributions and boost connection.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • People often make faulty judgments about why their partners behave the way they do.
  • Thinking that your partner’s negative behaviors are intentional is a major predictor of relationship distress.
  • Understanding your partner’s attachment style can prevent attributing their behavior to negative intentions.
  • You can use knowledge of your partner’s attachment style to preserve and build a healthier relationship.

Research with couples shows that one of the major factors underlying dissatisfaction and distress in romantic relationships is the idea that our partner is wounding us on purpose and with conscious awareness.

An attribution is a causal explanation we give for someone else’s behavior.

When negative, anxiety-inducing events occur, our human brains quickly move to find the explanation for the event. If you hear a loud noise in your house at night, you might feel impelled to go find the source. (Don’t do this if you are a character in a horror movie!) If you find the source of the noise and it is not a threat, your anxiety will go down. If you don’t find the source, your brain will stay active and keep searching for an explanation.

In relationships, if someone says something—or doesn’t say something—that makes your anxiety spike, your brain will similarly search for the source. For example, if your avoidant partner says nothing or doesn't attempt to comfort you when you share a disturbing experience at work, you may attribute (i.e., explain) their behavior as reflecting that they do not care about you. If you can’t find another explanation for their behavior, you will accept your conclusion as fact and react to it accordingly. In this case, your reaction might be to get more upset, point out their shortcomings, and accuse them of not caring.

People frequently make misattributions (faulty causal explanations) for things in ambiguous circumstances. Although your partner’s behaviors may be overtly observable, their motives may be ambiguous and need to be inferred. If you attribute your partner’s behavior to their not caring, or to their being "crazy" and overreactive, you are likely to act as if your thought is true and act on it. You might engage in protest behaviors that never get you the love you want. Or you might try to shut your partner down by leaving the room, telling them they are nuts, or shouting them down—and do you really think this will make an anxious partner feel calmer and more reassured?

Faulty attributions in relationships lead to self-fulfilling prophecies that make it much more likely you will get the exact behavior that you don’t want.

Why Attachment-Style Attributions Can Be a Solution

In couples therapy, I usually start by assessing each person’s attachment style and giving them feedback on the results in front of their partner. Knowing what your and your partner’s attachment styles are can prevent faulty attributions, “normalize” each person’s behaviors, and help you find solutions in your relationship.

To “normalize” a behavior does not mean you excuse, ignore, or accept that the behavior will continue. What it does mean is that you will be able to understand how a person with a specific attachment style typically processes events, experiences emotions, and behaves.

Using the example of an electrical circuit, it is normal for a person with an avoidant/dismissing attachment style to trip a circuit breaker when confronted with strong negative emotions, especially when they are being identified as the cause. When this happens, emotional energy stops flowing through the circuit and the person withdraws or goes cold and emotionally flat. That’s normal.

article continues after advertisement

Alternately, when a person with an anxious/preoccupied attachment style is confronted with the same type of negative emotional material, their circuit breaker does not blow. Instead, all that emotional energy keeps flowing through the circuit and overheating the system. The energy has to go somewhere, so it is usually expressed in the form of loud complaints, tears, or accusations that you are a cold person who doesn’t care—all normal for a person with this attachment style.

If you know your partner’s attachment style, you will be able to understand what is normal and avoid thinking that you are singled out for some special negative treatment. With practice, you should also be able to predict how a partner will react to the situations that confront them. This will help you derive an accurate attribution for your partner’s emotions and behaviors and give you more control over your own thoughts and emotional experiences in your interactions.

If you have knowledge of your own attachment style and that of your partner, you should be able to understand and anticipate the quality of your interactions. I rarely see two people with the same attachment style come in for therapy. Most often, one person is more avoidant, and the other is more anxious—and the ways that these dyads escalate in their conversations and conflicts typically follow very similar patterns.

Here is a caveat about attachment styles: Psychologists like me tell people the name of their style so that it can be understood more easily, but the reality underlying the styles is a bit more nuanced. No matter what your attachment style is, you have some level of both attachment avoidance and anxiety. Someone with a secure attachment style, for example, is likely to have low levels of avoidance and anxiety—but they still have them. So, someone might have a secure style but still be mildly elevated on how avoidant they are. I call this “secure leaning avoidant.” You can also be “secure leaning anxious.” Similarly, if you have a disorganized/fearful attachment style, you are likely to have high levels of both attachment avoidance and anxiety, but one is usually higher.

Here's how to start using this information in your relationship:

  1. Get an assessment of your and your partner’s attachment styles. Most psychologists trained in attachment theory can do this for you. When I do these assessments, I use three different measures: self-perception, close relationships, and romantic relationships. I caution against using one measure by itself from an online assessment because there is an inherent level of error involved in any personality assessment tool.
  2. Cross-check your results against descriptions of each of the attachment styles that can be found in published writings. And if you don’t have access to an assessment, you can read the descriptions and see if they line up with how you experience your partner and the type of parenting they received in childhood. (You can start by accessing my descriptions of secure, avoidant/dismissing, anxious/preoccupied, and disorganized/fearful styles.)
  3. Start to educate yourself on how couples with the different styles interact with each other.
  4. Once you know each other’s styles and have “normalized” them, you can start communicating better, understanding what the other person needs from you and setting expectations and boundaries. For example, if I am in a relationship with an avoidant person, I can understand why they shut down in serious discussion of feelings, but I am not going to accept them routinely ceasing to talk and walking out of the room. Or, I can understand why my anxious/preoccupied partner is feeling such intense emotions, but I still need to ask them to slow down, take shorter conversational turns, and calm themselves enough to let me speak.
article continues after advertisement

Once you take these steps, you can make more accurate and healthy attachment style attributions in your interactions, and thus preserve what is good about your relationship without assuming the worst about your partner. (This works in close friendships too.)

item.title: Teen Mental Health: Looking Beyond Screens and Social Media
item.description:
Adolescence

Teen Mental Health: Looking Beyond Screens and Social Media

Focusing only on social media can obscure other sources of teen distress.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Strong evidence to support that social media bans improve teen mental health is lacking.
  • Placing blame on social media for teen mental health may overlook other contributing factors.
  • Parents can help teens use social media responsibly by listening and setting reasonable limits.

Much has been written about the link between teen mental health challenges and screen time. Social media has been pointed to as a direct cause of distress among teens. For many teenagers, social media is so far integrated into their lives that they couldn’t possibly imagine going without it. Adolescents use social media for everything from increasing their social connections to reducing loneliness and finding safe spaces during difficult times in their lives. Even with these seemingly positive applications for social media, the social discourse remains unwavering in its stance that reliance on social media among young people is wreaking havoc on their mental stability.

However, as popular movies like “Toy Story 5” perpetuate this fear, casting dire warnings about the dangers of cyberbullying and social media addiction among adolescents and teens, some psychologists are taking another look at the connection between social media and teen mental health and arriving at some surprising conclusions: We may be barking up the wrong tree.

The “Sellability” of Scary Stories

Just like the urban myths that spread like wildfire in the 1980s about everything from razor blades in Halloween candy to Satanic messages in rock music, stories that put parents on edge about the safety and mental wellness of their children will always have a place in the zeitgeist. Today, the stories about the dangers of social media use for children prey on parents’ anxiety, and they are wildly effective.

Canadian psychologist Candice Odgers, who has studied adolescent mental health for 25 years, speaks to this effectiveness and how it may be leading parents to overreact to social media use, all the while overlooking other factors that can contribute to a breakdown in teen mental health. She sees a wide range of causes contributing to the deterioration of mental health among teens, and feels that the laser focus being given to social media could ultimately be detrimental in the search for solutions.

“The identification of social media as the culprit, as the biggest predictor of all the things that we worry about in our kids, is misleading, because it doesn’t show up that way in the vast majority of studies,” Odgers told The Guardian. “And it sucks all the air out of the room in terms of thinking about solutions.”

Nuances of Teen Mental Health and Social Media Use

In the wider conversation about social media and teen mental health, open communication between parents and children and nuance need to be front and center. Anything has the power to negatively impact a child’s mental stability, from a parent’s divorce to pressures stemming from a divided political climate. If we sweep the majority of these factors under the rug to highlight one component of a teen’s life and social interaction, we may be missing the mark on a societal level. Teens will be the ones to ultimately suffer from society’s myopic view.

Parents should monitor their children’s social media use and familiarize themselves with the various apps and trends. Placing limits on use, such as designating 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. as “phones off” time, can help teens learn how to regulate their social media use and find other outlets for socialization or entertainment. Parents should try to remain curious about their teen’s social media use, even though it can be easy to jump right to criticism. Check in with teens to see how they feel about social media. Lastly, it’s important for adults to model good habits for the teens in their lives. A family-wide media plan can help all members of the family have a healthier relationship with technology.

Ultimately, as social media platforms evolve and become a more significant part of daily life, parents and teens will have to learn how to live with the technology. There is a notable lack of strong scientific evidence to support that social media bans for teenagers improve mental health. Blanket bans and loud discourse about teen tech use can shift focus away from other systemic issues impacting teen mental health, such as family dysfunction or economic insecurity. By making social media the one and only scapegoat, teen mental health is liable to continue to decline.

What may be more productive for parents is comprehensive guidance that considers social media as part of modern life. We should also, as a society, continue to support common-sense safety measures around social media use for teens.

Social media is not going anywhere. As years go by and technology improves, these platforms may play an even more important role in our social interactions, businesses, and family connections. Learning to apply nuance to these conversations can help parents understand the teen perspective on social media and help teens learn how to use social media responsibly.

item.title: Healing Injuries and the Injuries of Healing
item.description:
Therapy

Healing Injuries and the Injuries of Healing

Healing can hurt as much as being wounded.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Leaving a toxic relationship can expose losses that were postponed for years.
  • Attachment does not disappear just because someone recognizes they were mistreated.
  • Healing can hurt. Some new pain may signal that recovery is underway.
  • Grief, guilt, and fear can be considered adaptive injuries.

A challenging aspect of working with patients is adjusting their expectations of healing. Many assume, or desperately wish to believe, that healing means feeling less pain every day. Telling them that healing itself contains pain and brings a different kind of injury can be difficult. Let’s call these adaptive injuries: injuries that actually indicate that healing is taking place.

Let's listen to Elena. The first night after leaving her marriage, she slept with the hallway light on. There was no one to criticize how she folded towels, question why she smiled at a message, or ask whether her dress was “appropriate for a mother.”

For 16 years, her husband, Mark, corrected her stories at dinner, laughed when she expressed an opinion—very often in front of their families and friends. He called her sensitive whenever she cried. After arguments, he could ignore her for days.

She learned to rehearse conversations before speaking. She deleted harmless texts to avoid interrogation. She stopped seeing friends who “put ideas in her head.” Eventually, she believed the problem was her inability to keep him happy.

In therapy, she at first wanted techniques to communicate better. Instead, she discovered how much of her marriage revolved around anticipating Mark’s reactions. Her therapist did not instruct her to leave but they explored her fear, her financial dependence, and the difference between compromise and coercive control. Six months later, she signed a lease on a small apartment.

She imagined freedom would feel like breathing after years underwater. Instead, she found herself crying in supermarket aisles because she could not decide what cereal to buy. Without Mark's approval or objections, even trivial decisions felt dangerous.

When you leave the darkness, the first thing that hurts is the light.

Their friends stopped calling. Some believed Mark’s account that therapy had made her selfish. Others preferred not to choose sides. The family home remained his; her daughtet, Lucy, moved between two addresses, carrying a schoolbag that never seemed unpacked.

One Sunday, she refused to leave her father’s house. “Dad says you broke the family because you wanted to be happy,” she told her mother over the phone.

Elena wanted to tell her about every humiliation, every silent dinner, every apology extracted from her. But Lucy was a child, not a witness she could summon to defend herself.

In therapy she asked, “If healing is supposed to save me, why has it cost me everyone?”

What Elena mourned was complicated: Mark’s good mornings, the holidays, their shared jokes. She missed having someone to call when the car broke down. She missed the family photographs in which everyone appeared happy. She even missed the version of herself who could believe the marriage would improve if she tried harder. And she felt ashamed of missing him.

article continues after advertisement

Her therapist told her, “Leaving a prison doesn’t necessarily mean you enter freedom. Sometimes you enter a bigger prison labeled ‘freedom’ whose rules are unknown to you, and you miss the smaller prison. However, one day, you wake up and notice that stops. That is the day you know you are free.”

Over time, she began to understand that attachment does not disappear when someone recognizes mistreatment, and that recovery doesn't guarantee immediate peace.

Therapy introduced its own difficult work. As Elena learned to notice anger, she sometimes snapped at Lucy. When she started saying no, she occasionally mistook every request for a threat. Freedom was unfamiliar, and her first attempts to use it were imperfect.

A year later, Lucy came to the apartment and asked if they could bake a cake. Elena opened a cupboard stocked with ingredients she had chosen herself. The daughter who once watched her mother disappear now watched her make decisions, hesitate, and sometimes change her mind.

Elena still grieved the marriage, and some relationships remained fractured. Healing had freed her from one kind of injury while leaving her to bear others: the grief of an imagined future, the guilt of disrupting a family, and the frightening responsibility of becoming herself.

Recovery was teaching her that being visible could hurt, too.

item.title: Blood Donation and the Burden of Memory
item.description:
Religion

Blood Donation and the Burden of Memory

A Jehovah’s Witnesses' policy shift expands choice and reopens old wounds.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Witnesses may now decide to accept blood components and reinfusion while whole blood remains prohibited.
  • Shunning and lost relationships can outlast a changed doctrinal rule.
  • Therapists can explore faith, fear, autonomy, and loss without steering a client’s beliefs.

Until this September, Jehovah’s Witnesses were taught to refuse transfusions of donor whole blood and its four main components: red cells, white cells, plasma, and platelets.

On September 18, 2026, the organization made those four components a personal decision, changing the decades-old policy so that each member may choose whether to accept them from another person, use their own stored blood, or donate blood specifically to provide components or fractions. Despite these changes, whole blood transfusions from another person remain prohibited, and the organization says they continue to regard blood as sacred.

This reform has been celebrated by many as a move toward a safer future for these religious adherents, but the weight of past decisions and losses on members and ex-members alike remains.

The Moral Weight of the Earlier Rule

The Witnesses’ opposition to transfusions dates back to early days with several shifts in teaching. For example, in 1961, an unrepentant recipient could be disfellowshipped and shunned for accepting a whole blood infusion.

By 2000, the organization explicitly prohibited the four main components and, in March 2026, amended the doctrine so that making use of one’s own blood, including storage and reinfusion, would become “a matter of conscience,” essentially meaning that an individual could decide whether to accept their own blood products. This September’s announcement extended that discretion to the four donor components and the patient’s own stored blood.

Refusing blood products throughout this history has led to the deaths of many Witnesses. The organization acknowledged deaths after blood loss and, in a 1994 magazine, described a teenager who died after refusing transfusions that might have extended his life. There is, of course, no reliable worldwide count telling us how many a different policy would have saved, and doctrine certainly cannot establish whether a transfusion would have saved a particular person.

Despite this, I have counseled former Witnesses since 1989, including parents who later struggled with their role in a child’s refusal of blood, and this uncertainty does not lessen their grief.

The Instability of Certainty

For a member facing surgery, relief may now coexist with painful cognitive dissonance, a discomfort from seemingly conflicting beliefs or experiences due to these doctrinal changes. How could a component that once carried a grave religious consequence now be left to conscience? Others may find the explanation consistent with their faith, or sincerely decline every blood product. Rather than prescribing a certain response to the recent news, we, and especially clinicians, should listen.

article continues after advertisement

For someone bereaved as a result of past policy, the changes may create a sense of moral injury, best understood as severe distress when an action clashes with one’s morals. A Witness may replay a hospital conversation and ask, “Could they have chosen differently? Would they have lived?” Within clinical practice, such questions should be treated carefully, and without assuming any sort of verdict on motives or a claim that a different choice certainly would have saved a life.

The earlier threat of losing one’s congregation has also shaped the setting in which choices were made. The organization now says such medical decisions are private and the congregation will not judge a member for making their own personal medical decisions. While this new assurance is certainly meaningful, this newfound permission does not reveal with certainty what a particular patient wants, especially if an older medical directive still records a refusal written under the previous rule.

Shifting Relationships

Shunning within Witness doctrine means deliberately limiting social contact after someone’s removal from the community, and members do not socialize with removed people, although they may greet them at meetings, and household family ties may sometimes continue.

What this means is that someone who accepted a blood component under an earlier rule might have faced congregational consequences while the same choice is now permitted. That reversal may deepen an estranged person’s sense of unfairness, and it certainly does not restore community bonds or relationships immediately—if at all. Studies of former Witnesses link ostracism with struggles over identity and belonging, alongside varied coping and growth.

This ambiguous loss—the grief of having someone alive but socially unavailable—can be especially hard to explain to outsiders. For those who have been shunned, this loss may sit beside grief, anger at an old rule, love for relatives who remain Witnesses, and genuine hope that the organization keeps reforming.

Careful Clinical Responses

Therapists should ask about a client’s religious history and current ties when they are relevant to the client’s distress. By cult-aware care, I mean noticing how authority, information, and the possible loss of relationships can affect decisions, without assuming that a client lacks agency or telling them what to believe. For current Witnesses, ask what the policy meant to them then, what it means now, and whom they feel safe talking to.

article continues after advertisement

If treatment is approaching, clinicians can encourage the patient to review any old directive with their medical team. The American College of Surgeons advises speaking with Witness patients privately, checking their own wishes, and providing a space with freedom from pressure. A therapist can help a client put fears and values into words to help the patient and medical team make the medical decision. Therapy can also make room for grief without turning uncertainty into blame.

We should want religious groups to correct rules that may have caused harm. However, welcoming this change while taking earlier suffering seriously and considering the effects on past members all deserve the same consideration.

item.title: When Does a Fetish Become Objectification?
item.description:
Sex

When Does a Fetish Become Objectification?

We need to treat partners as whole people—not just a way to act out a fantasy.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • A preference becomes objectification when a desired trait eclipses the person as a whole.
  • Ethical fetish exploration puts a partner’s health and comfort above sexual gratification.
  • Disclosing a fetish should invite understanding, not pressure a partner to fulfill it.

I have a friend who’s really into dating highly educated people, with three of her last four partners having had PhDs. Another friend is a white girl who is always pursuing a person of color every time we go out. One of my clients, who has a sneeze fetish, specifically seeks out women boasting what he considers “cute sneezes.” Another client is a self-proclaimed devotee: someone who is aroused by disability. Their last three partners have been wheelchair users. I tend to be into nerdy Jewish boys who have lived at their parents’ houses for too long.

When it comes to whom we are attracted to, where is the line between pursuing your preferences and objectifying people? And is there a way to ethically fetishize someone?

The point at which a preference tips into a problem is hard to identify, but there is a question you can ask to figure it out: Are you considering the person as a whole human, or is the rest of them just a vehicle for the thing you’re really into? Because the other, rather obvious, but wildly underutilized rule for how to be both decent and horny is to treat people as... people. Like, whole humans who lead independent and complicated lives independent of your sexual desires.

An Example of the Human-First Approach to Fetish

Meet Robin, a smoking enthusiast. Broad, compelling, and thoughtful, he comes off a bit like a football coach with a smoking fetish and an interest in 19th-century literature. An alluring woman with pink glasses and a cigarette hanging from her lips stared past us from a picture frame behind him on our Zoom call, underscoring his success in integrating the sexy act of smoking into his everyday life. He drew her, as well as many other beautiful smoking portraits, as a way to explore and understand his rather unusual muse.

He chooses his words with care. It’s obvious that he has spent a lot of time thinking about his fetish, making sense of it to himself and patiently explaining it to others.

“Including your mama?” I inquired. “Yes, of course,” he responded. His fastidious choice of words and kind but firm affect make him an effective—if somewhat understated—ambassador for smoking fetishes.

His fetish began when he saw George Michael’s “Freedom! ’90” music video, which he described as “incredibly smoky and sexy.” Like many fetishes, Robin’s fascination with smoking goes back to early childhood, and as his sexuality developed, so too did his eroticization of it.

He shared matter-of-factly that “the highest anybody could be is an eight if they aren’t smoking.” He enjoys “smoking as an enhancement of femininity, smoking as a tool of seduction, the sensuality of smoking. The taste, smell, feel, sound, and tension.” As with so much of what we find hot, it’s hard to describe in detail what makes it so alluring—you get it, or you don’t.

article continues after advertisement

As is common, Robin’s arousal is related to someone else smoking, which we obviously know isn’t great for your body. Although having a couple drags of a smoke during a sexual encounter probably isn’t going to give you cancer, being with a partner who encourages you to smoke for their own pleasure can affect your health in a serious way. The same way dating a boy who’s super into candy hasn’t at all helped my quest to grate that gouda on my stomach.

Robin gushed, “In high school, I convinced my girlfriend to smoke for me during foreplay,” which was exciting for both of them. After all, smoking and teenagers go together like coffee and cigarettes. But as he grew older and his partners became more health-conscious, incorporating smoking into sex got more and more dicey. He eventually managed to both marry a smoker and refrain from divulging his smoking fetish to her. This guy is no joke.

A few years into their marriage, Robin’s wife quit smoking. Still in the processing-shame-and-secretly-drawing-smoking-women-in-notebooks phase of his fetish exploration, he didn’t share anything but encouragement. After all, nicotine is a damn hard thing to drop, and he’s a kind man and supportive husband. Yet, the smoking fetish smoldered in his loins.

Years into their marriage, and a long time after she’d quit, he finally got up the courage to share his desire with his wife. He was very clear that he didn’t expect any change in her behavior—he just wanted her to know about this part of him. Of her own volition, she expressed interest in creating clear and agreed-upon boundaries to explore erotic smoking. They took it slowly, from her holding a smoke during sexual activity to her taking a drag or two once or twice a year during sex. Robin was thrilled to be able to explore this fetish with his wife, and he shared that outside of these stand-alone experiences, his wife has not started smoking again.

Of course, if she were a less strong woman, having smoking images around the house and taking the occasional drag could be enough to get her addicted again. Does this make Robin’s behavior unethical?

No. Robin thinks about his fetish within the context of his relationship as a whole, valuing his wife’s needs as much as his own. They married because of mutual love and admiration—not because Robin was fiending after smoky sex. It was only after they’d settled into a happy life together that he started a conversation about his fetish, and only after she’d assured him that this was cool with her that they created a plan for how to explore it.

article continues after advertisement

Every step of the way, he put her love on top (thanks, Beyoncé, for always helping us find the words)—he honored her and their relationship above his need to realize his fetish. There were so many ways for him to not do this: He could have tried to pressure her into smoking during sex by threatening to leave; he could have tried to trick her into smoking full-time again; he could have told her that he’d only love her if she smoked like Tony Soprano. Instead, he put his fetish in the context of his relationship, and they found a path forward together.

That’s the human-first approach. Any desire that carries risk—physical, emotional, or otherwise—demands that humans be prioritized over pleasure. This applies just as much to a one-night stand as it does for your partner of 52 years.

When you are disclosing a potentially dangerous fetish, I want you to ask yourself: Have I shared my fetish without an agenda, or am I secretly hoping to persuade them? Can I accept a no without punishment or withdrawal (or bringing it up every three days until my partner feels pressured into exploring it)? Have I made it clear—explicitly—that their comfort matters more than my arousal? The takeaway is simple: Express your desires clearly and prioritize your partner’s health and comfort more than your own pleasure.

Robin had the advantage of wanting to realize his fetish with his loving wife, whom he would presumably do nearly anything for (he gave that vibe). But we need to value the humanity of our casual hookup partners in the same way. Inconvenient as it may seem, "randos" are human beings who are far above being used as instruments of your lust. Being a good person to those we don’t know, as the fire of desire rages inside us, takes discipline. It’s worth it.

item.title: When We Can 'Be More Bird,' We Recover a Primal Navigation
item.description:
Animal Behavior

When We Can 'Be More Bird,' We Recover a Primal Navigation

A hawk-guided journey gifts us with forgotten wisdom we need in today's world.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Any living thing can teach us, if we only look, attend, and connect.
  • We can find our own way to fly: Nature inspires profound, navigational wisdom.
  • We have ancient wisdom. We can learn from organisms and systems that pre-date us by millennia.

“Once upon a time, when women were birds, there was the simple understanding that to sing at dawn and to sing at dusk was to heal the world through joy. The birds still remember what we have forgotten, that the world is meant to be celebrated.” –Terry Tempest Williams

Candida with Bird, a Harris hawk.
Source: Jesse Wilkinson / Candida Meyrick, used with permission

Every now and then, a book opens a portal to our primal connection to Earth, something we need more of in this time of rapidly destabilizing planetary systems.

Be More Bird, Life Lessons From a Hawk, by Candida Meyrick, is such a portal. Candida is a falconer, novelist, mother, and cancer survivor, whose experiences with her Harris Hawk provide a window into the numinous, extraordinary potentials of connecting with, and creating with, the more-than-human world.

Rachel Clark: Could you briefly describe what beckoned you to write Be More Bird?

Candida Meyrick: The answer to this has a long root! I’ve always written and always painted. My mother is a writer, my father was a painter, and I have long tussled with individuating myself with these totemic forces.

Bird’s arrival allowed me to rise—to see the larger landscape of my life and the foolishness of struggling within reductive dualities. Bird for me is a cosmic weaver, moving with grace between opposing states.

She delivered a hawk-inspired point of brisk decision: Write this! Also: Paint this! Just make the attempt. Because if you don’t, what are you, exactly?

Bird and Candida
Source: Jesse Wilkinson / Candida Meyrick, used with permission

RC: What first inspired you to welcome Bird into your life?

CM: I had had cancer five years earlier, which offered me the gift of saying Yes to things I might otherwise not have had the courage to accept. So when my children became interested in birds of prey, I said, why not? It spoke to a yearning buried deep in my childhood, which I had abandoned. By their wholehearted involvement in the acquiring, training, and flying of Bird, my children unwittingly performed a life-changing miracle of healing, ushering in a process of ongoing transformation. There are resonances here with shamanic and family constellation therapies.

article continues after advertisement

RC: You have a way of writing about Bird that evokes our natural kinship to the more-than-human world. How did this sense of kinship begin for you? How has it evolved?

Bird takes flight from her perch with Candida
Source: Jesse Wilkinson / Candida Meyrick, used with permission

CM: This sense of kinship began the moment I first glimpsed her—caught her eye. That combination of power and terror—the fact that strength and vulnerability were in some way co-dependent was a revelation.

So I set myself an impossible task. To try to say this unsayable thing—to underline the reality of this kinship. Not through hubris but humility, because I knew that the attempt was doomed to failure: It could only be experienced in the moment.

Realizing this, I remember feeling a huge burst of lucid power—a sort of upsurge of spiritual revelation: just to make the attempt to convey how she had crossed the boundaries of species to move me in this way would be enough. Words were a poor vehicle—but the best I had. Just to make the attempt overwhelmed me with that sense of kinship with all living things.

This is of course ancient wisdom. And it’s well that we should learn from organisms and systems that pre-date us by millennia and will likely outlive us. It’s weird that we don’t.

RC: What inspired you to write the book as a series of life lessons for people?

Bird and Candida watch the horizon.
Source: Jesse Wilkinson / Candida Meyrick, used with permission

CM: I was gripped by the desire to convey what she had taught me. I didn’t want to declare "This is what falconry is" but more "This is what I have witnessed, what I have learnt"—and by extension suggest what any living thing can teach us, if we only look, attend, connect.

When I had cancer, I spent hours in a hammock between a venerable oak on one side and a huge ash on the other. Those trees were my healers. How to explain that? I’d have to write a book to fully articulate it. Learning those lessons from nature at that low point in my life set me on the path where I met Bird.

article continues after advertisement

RC: What were the gifts for you of writing Be More Bird?

Bird returns to Candida.
Source: Jesse Wilkinson / Candida Meyrick, used with permission

CM: Just the attempt to articulate what she has shown me has given me the gift of self-respect—honoring the child in me, asserting what she believes in and cares about.

It also feels like a form of precious groundwork: I have cleared my path, planted my values, accepted the sound of my own voice when it states what really matters to me. Now, everything has Bird at its heart: she is my touchstone and spirit-guide. The full articulation of this will take a lifetime.

RC: What gifts do you hope it offers to readers?

CM: I set out to write Be More Bird with a far more outward intention than with my novels—in the spirit of humble gift-giving and intense gratitude. That I was still alive to fly this bird and write this story was joyous.

It was also a love letter to my children. The act of writing this story became a discovery of how maternal love is, in essence, liberating. I love that the book might be a gift of strength and purpose, a revelation of joy in adversity, an underlining of the power of mothering—what it means to "be more bird."

item.title: Surviving the Adderall Shortage, Still, in 2026
item.description:
ADHD

Surviving the Adderall Shortage, Still, in 2026

Four years in, here's what actually keeps a prescription filled.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • The FDA listed amphetamine mixed salts in shortage in October 2022. It is still listed in September 2026.
  • The DEA raised amphetamine production quotas in October 2025 and again in the final 2026 notice.
  • National data show switching more than stopping; alternative stimulant fills rose 8.0 points.
  • Children insured by Medicaid were affected more than commercially insured children.

The FDA added amphetamine mixed salts to its drug shortage list in October 2022. The listing is still active in September 2026, which makes this one of the longest-running access problems for any commonly prescribed psychiatric medication.

I treat ADHD and I study how these medications get prescribed. Over four years my patients have worked out a set of habits that keep prescriptions filled, and those habits have been more useful than anything in the policy literature. What follows is that playbook, along with the arithmetic underneath the shortage, because a patient who understands the machine argues with it more effectively.

Where Supply Actually Stands

The shortage has improved without ending. Teva currently lists amphetamine mixed salts extended-release 10 mg and 15 mg capsules on back order with release estimated in early September 2026, and the 20 mg capsule estimated in late October 2026. Immediate-release tablets remain inconsistent from strength to strength and from pharmacy to pharmacy.

Three forces sustain it. Amphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance, so the DEA sets a national production ceiling each year. Manufacturing is concentrated among a small number of generic producers, so a single company's problem propagates across the whole market. And prescribing has risen substantially since 2020, particularly among adults.

The quota picture has moved. The DEA raised d-amphetamine production by roughly 25% in October 2025, and in the final 2026 quota notice published January 5, 2026, set aggregate d,l-amphetamine production at 24,234,443 grams, about 14% above the level it had originally proposed, following more than 5,000 public comments. Methylphenidate was held at 2025 levels. Supply for several amphetamine strengths improved as a result. Supply has not equilibrated, and the FDA has announced no resolution date.

The practical consequence is that this is a strength-by-strength, pharmacy-by-pharmacy problem, and the patients who fare best treat it that way.

The Playbook

Call the pharmacy before the prescription is sent. This is the single highest-yield habit on the list. Ask your prescriber to hold the prescription until you have confirmed that a specific pharmacy has your strength in stock. A controlled-substance prescription sent to an empty pharmacy is stuck there until someone transfers it, and transfers take days.

Ask about equivalent configurations. Two 10 mg tablets deliver the same dose as one 20 mg tablet. Pharmacies frequently have one strength and lack another, and a prescriber can write the same total daily dose in whatever units exist. In my practice this one conversation rescues more fills than every other item here combined.

article continues after advertisement

Know your molecule's relatives. Adderall is mixed amphetamine salts. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is a close relative with generics now available, and dextroamphetamine is another. Moving within the amphetamine family is a small clinical step. Moving to the methylphenidate family is a larger one, though it is sometimes the right call. None of this is a do-it-yourself project, and all of it is a reasonable conversation to request.

Work both the chains and the independents. Large chains can query nearby stores' inventory, which saves hours of phone calls. Independent pharmacies sometimes hold supply the chains lack, because distributors allocate to them differently. Patients who build a relationship with one independent pharmacist often stop having this problem altogether.

Do not stretch a supply by skipping doses silently. A planned dose reduction is occasionally reasonable and should involve your prescriber. An unplanned stop returns symptoms at full strength, and driving, work, and school all register it. If a gap is genuinely unavoidable, say so out loud to your prescriber, because bridging options exist.

Mind the calendar. Controlled-substance rules restrict early refills, so the buffer you need has to be built deliberately. If you are traveling, or your pharmacy's delivery day is Thursday, the refill conversation starts a week out rather than on the morning the bottle empties.

What the Shortage Has Done to Treatment

For most of its duration, the harm from this shortage was anecdotal. In 2025 that changed. He and colleagues used national dispensing data to compare children and adolescents who had been taking immediate-release Adderall before October 2022 against matched controls (He S, McCabe SE, Conti RM, Chua KP, Pediatrics 2025;155(6):e2025070777). The numbers deserve to be read closely. Children previously on Adderall IR showed a 1.9 percentage point greater decrease in Adderall IR dispensing than controls, alongside an 8.0 percentage point greater increase in dispensing of other stimulants. Outright discontinuation rose by 1.2 percentage points. Switching to non-stimulant medication barely moved, at 0.08 percentage points. The effects were larger among children insured by Medicaid than among commercially insured children.

article continues after advertisement

The dominant signal is substitution. Most children stayed on stimulant treatment and moved to whichever molecule was available, which is a real credit to the prescribers and pharmacists who absorbed that work. However, a 1.2 percentage point increase in discontinuation across a national population describes a large absolute number of children who stopped treatment, and the Medicaid gradient means that the families with the least capacity to absorb a disruption absorbed the most of it.

Interrupted stimulant treatment carries consequences beyond the return of symptoms. My colleagues and I have written about the protective side of this ledger, arguing in an editorial on real-world outcomes that reducing serious externalizing outcomes is an important public health benefit and is only part of the story (Sultan RS, Saunders DC, Veenstra-VanderWeele J, JAMA Psychiatry 2025;82:757-758). In earlier work on adolescents with ADHD, we documented the adverse behaviors and comorbid conditions that cluster around the diagnosis (Sultan RS, Liu SM, Hacker KA, Olfson M, J Adolesc Health 2021;68(2):284-291). Continuity is the mechanism through which treatment delivers those benefits, which is the reason the fill itself belongs inside the treatment plan rather than beside it.

What I Tell Patients

Treat the pharmacy like part of your care team, because for the duration of this shortage it is. Build a week of buffer into every refill. Learn the two or three strengths that would work for you instead of the one you are used to, so that a substitution conversation takes two minutes rather than two visits. And tell your prescriber the moment a fill fails, rather than after the bottle is empty, because almost every workaround above requires lead time.

This shortage will end. Quotas and manufacturing will eventually meet demand, and the 2026 numbers suggest that process is underway. Until it finishes, the patients who do best are the ones who treat the fill as part of the treatment, and the prescribers who do best are the ones who expect the phone call.
