item.title: How to Deal With the 'Foodie Call' in Dating
item.description:
Mating

How to Deal With the 'Foodie Call' in Dating

Could inflation be feeding this dating trend?

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • A "foodie call" is when someone has no real romantic interest in you but still accepts a dinner date.
  • The motivation in a "foodie call" is to just get a free meal or at least try a new restaurant.
  • If you want to prevent "foodie calls," you might suggest a more casual "lower-stakes" first date.
A foodie call is when someone who has no real romantic interest in you still goes on a dinner date with you just for a free meal or at least the opportunity to try a particular restaurant or type of food.
Source: Julia Filirovska / Pexels

Have you ever been on a date where the other person seems much more interested in the mussels than your muscles, the crab legs than your legs, and the chicken satay rather than what you have to say? Then you could be on that person's "foodie call."

What Is a 'Foodie Call'?

A foodie call is when someone who has no real romantic interest in you still goes on a dinner date with you just for a free meal or at least the opportunity to try a particular restaurant or type of food. You essentially could become that person's one-time meal ticket. And based on previous studies, like two of them published in a 2019 issue of the scientific journal Social Psychological and Personality Science, it can be more than a one-time experience for those in the dating arena, with 23 percent and 33 percent of the women surveyed in those studies, respectively, admitting to having done foodie calls.

The studies found that those regularly doing foodie calls were significantly more likely to score higher on the "Dark Triad" characteristics—namely Machiavellianism (the tendency to manipulate others for self-benefit), psychopathy (the lack of empathy), and narcissism (an inflated sense of entitlement), as David Ludden, Ph.D., covered in 2019 in Psychology Today. That, of course, doesn't mean that all foodie callers are that way. And while these studies did specifically survey females, women aren't necessarily the only ones who might do the foodie-calling thing. Anyone who can get some or all of their meal paid for by a date might have food for thought in such a way when it comes to dating.

Could 'Date-flation' Be Increasing the Risk of 'Foodie Calls'?

Fast forward from 2019 to 2026, with inflation having pushed prices in the United States up by 31.03 percent, based on the Consumer Price Index. I've already written about date-flation in "A Funny Bone to Pick," with the cost of a typical all-in date rising from $168 to $189 over just a one-year period from 2025 to 2026. This could make it even more likely to run into foodie callers when you are on the dating trail mix. At the very least, it could make a foodie call more expensive for you.

Of course, maybe you are fine with paying for someone's meal when that person isn't really paying any interest in you. Perhaps you're banking on the possibility that you can change the foodie caller's mind about you on the date and pull the sweet out of the sour. A foodie call can be sweet and dandy if both parties are completely fine with it.

article continues after advertisement

Lack of Genuine Engagement Could Suggest a 'Foodie Call'

However, if you view foodie calls as a waste of your resources and—more importantly—your time, then you may want to stay aware of some possible red flags or perhaps red velvet cake flags. One is a lack of genuine interest and engagement before and especially during the dinner date, like when your date seems less interested in maintaining eye contact and more interested in maintaining pie à la mode contact. Your date should show some genuine interest in getting to know you better.

The word "genuine" is key here because seasoned foodie callers could be adept at faking interest in you and engaging with you in a formulaic and performative manner. In fact, foodie callers may even love bomb you—primarily with the hope that you will Birria Bomb them back. So, beware of inauthenticity.

Too Much Focus on Where You'll Be Dining Could Suggest a 'Foodie Call'

Another red velvet cake flag is the other person focusing way too much on where you'll be dining. Sure, your date might have very specific dietary preferences or even requirements due to food allergies or other medical reasons. But if that individual seems intent on eating at a very specific restaurant—especially an expensive one—without a plausible reason despite your suggesting other restaurants, then you've gotta wonder.

A History of 'Foodie Calling' Raises the Risk of a 'Foodie Call'

Then there's the "pasta" possibly predicting the future consideration. If the person is known for regularly doing foodie calls before, then sure, you may be an exception. But what makes you think so?

A foodie caller may even have a polished playbook for such dates, such as checking when Chef Sussudio will actually be working at a restaurant and then coordinating the date to match that day and time. In general, if you feel like you are no more than part of a process or just an appetizer when the main course is the main dinner course, you could be right.

article continues after advertisement

Reluctance to Go on a More Casual First Date Might Suggest a 'Foodie Call'

One way to prevent a "foodie call" is to suggest a more casual first date—such as meeting for coffee, dessert, or a walk—and see how the other person reacts. After all, isn't the ultimate purpose of a first date to determine whether the two of you may be a good fit and whether both of you might want at least a second helping of each other? If the other person expresses reluctance to go on such a lower-stakes first date, then you could be dealing with a foodie caller.

In general, it's OK to communicate any concerns that you may have as long as you remain appropriately respectful. For example, if the cost of a dinner is going to be a problem for you, consider being honest and straightforward about it and discussing more affordable options. Don't try to be who you are not. If the other person is going to reject you as a result of you being you, then it probably wasn't a good match anyway.

Don't let the foodie calling out there leave you with a sour taste for dating in general, though. Remember the aforementioned studies also suggested that a majority of people out there aren't doing the foodie-calling thing. And even if you do get flambé-d here and there by different bad dating experiences, try not to generalize and stereotype. Stay open to possibilities. You never know when you might run into the person who is just your taste and wants to get things cooking with you and not just the food that you have to offer.

item.title: Why a Sexist 'SNL' Monologue Matters
item.description:
Gender

Why a Sexist 'SNL' Monologue Matters

Misogyny is never just a joke.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Sexist humour does not exist in a vacuum. Instead, it reflects and shapes social norms.
  • Saying "it's just a joke" overlooks the psychological impact of sexist humour.
  • Men play a crucial role in challenging misogyny when it appears in public life.

In the space of a few days, two male public figures offered radically different messages about women. On "Saturday Night Live," comedian Shane Gillis used his monologue to discuss women’s gym wear and announce that he "didn’t know women just dressed like whores now."

Shortly after this, actor, writer, and comedian Dan Levy responded on Instagram, challenging Gillis and arguing that a woman's choice of clothing does not justify degrading sexual labels. Levy went on to highlight the misogyny of the monologue and argued that more men should challenge the objectification of women rather than remain silent, especially when it occurs on a widely viewed public stage like SNL.

So Why Does This Matter?

You could argue that this is simply comedy doing what it's always done—provoking, offending, and pushing boundaries. But context matters: Women don’t experience these jokes in a world free from harassment, objectification, sexual violence, and abuse. They experience them in a culture where being reduced to a body, a sexual stereotype, or an object of male commentary remains commonplace.

The same week that public discussion focused on allegations emerging from Cornell University—including reports that an unconscious young woman was reportedly offered up for sex in a fraternity Snapchat—it seems reasonable to ask whether a primetime comedy show joking about women as "whores" moves us forward or simply reinforces problematic attitudes.

Humour Is Never Just Humour

When people defend controversial jokes, the phrase we hear most often is that it's "just a joke." As if failing to laugh means you lack a sense of humour and the problem lies with you, rather than the person making the so-called joke.

Psychologically, however, humour is rarely "just" anything. Weber et al. (2023) found that exposure to sexist comedy had a detrimental effect on women’s cognitive performance, regardless of their own receptiveness to humour.

Likewise, Argüello‐Gutiérrez et al. (2023) reported that women exposed to sexist humour consistently felt significantly higher levels of anger, displeasure, and offence than their male counterparts. This was particularly interesting, given that Argüello‐Gutiérrez et al. found that both sexes were exposed to such humour at a much higher level than expected, even when simply going about their day. It suggests that far from existing on the margins of social life, sexist humour functions as a routine and normalised feature of many women's everyday experiences. Against this backdrop, the question is not whether one more joke about women being 'whores' matters, but why so many people think it doesn't.

article continues after advertisement

Humour is a valuable and rewarding part of life, which is consistently associated with positive wellbeing (Korock et al. 2026). It helps to signal group membership by establishing what is (and is not) acceptable to laugh at. It identifies who belongs, who doesn't, and who is expected to tolerate being the target. We laugh because we recognise that others around us find it acceptable, and that emboldens us to join in.

In other words, humour helps to create the culture that we all live in, including the social rules about what is and isn’t acceptable within that culture. That may seem harmless to those making the jokes, but for those who find themselves repeatedly cast as the punchline, the cumulative effect can be exhausting.

In 2016, Perez and Greene examined the response to a rape joke directed at a female audience member during a live performance in Hollywood. Their analysis found that the dominant framing and interpretation of rape jokes reinforced patriarchal ideologies among those present and encouraged denial of the real-world implications of misogynistic humour. This effect was found to be particularly true in cases where the comedian or their audience subsequently defended the joke.

Of course, that doesn’t mean that everyone who laughed at Shane Gillis' monologue is misogynistic. Nor does it mean that one joke causes violence against women. However, the idea that humour exists in a vacuum, detached from wider social beliefs and behaviours, is just as difficult to defend.

Two Models of Masculinity

This situation presents two very different models of masculinity. The first, the monologue by Gillis, is rooted in objectification. It works by inviting the audience to evaluate women's bodies and clothing, and use those judgments to create derogatory labels for women. The underlying premise is that women are there to be observed, assessed, categorised, and judged. Their role in the joke is not to be fully human participants in society, but simply objects of male commentary.

article continues after advertisement

The second model, exemplified by Levy's response, is rooted in accountability. Rather than inviting audiences to scrutinise women, he asked men to scrutinise themselves and the attitudes that make objectification seem normal. He asked why some men feel entitled to describe women using degrading sexual labels and then explicitly framed misogyny as a men's issue rather than a women's issue. He argued that men need to defend women more actively and challenge objectification when they encounter it. In these two very different models of masculinity, only one leaves women better off.

For decades, women have described the harms of sexual objectification, harassment, double standards, and violence. Yet such concerns are often dismissed as overreactions or interpreted as evidence that women "can't take a joke." When men challenge misogyny, the conversation starts to change, and the issue can no longer be reduced to female sensitivity. Instead, it becomes a discussion about norms, respect, and accountability. Speaking out may not make life easier for the men who do it, but it helps create safer, fairer environments for the women who live and work alongside them.

item.title: Why Is There a Duality Between Suffering and Hastening Death?
item.description:
Fear

Why Is There a Duality Between Suffering and Hastening Death?

Rethinking end-of-life suffering, euthanasia, and palliative care.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Existential fear of death involves concerns about nonexistence, separation, and unfulfilled life goals.
  • Euthanasia and physician-assisted suicide involve ethical, clinical, and legal considerations.
  • Psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy and palliative sedation may be ethical ways to help patients face death.

Several years of studying cancer biology in the lab did not make me ignore the suffering and pain of cancer patients in hospitals. My father loved life and hoped to live longer. He died from esophageal cancer. The doctors were disappointed with his outcome and recommended that he go home without telling him that he had deadly cancer. A couple of weeks before his death, he lost the ability to move, eat, and drink. He fell into a coma-like state a few days before passing away. However, when I said to him several minutes before his death, "If you hear me, push my hand," he weakly squeezed my hand. He appeared to remain aware of me until the end and faced his inevitable fate.

A philosophical question: Why must we endure the suffering caused by diseases or death without selecting them?

Almost all living beings have an instinctual intention to survive and a fear of death. In this regard, existential fear of death in humans is associated with an individual's awareness of their own mortality; however, not all human beings experience this awareness in the same way, nor do all anxieties regarding death necessarily stem from consciousness. The fear of death should not be reduced to the fear of pain or the process of death. Humans may feel anxious because they fear nonexistence, separation from loved ones, and the loss of their life goals. Clinical evidence revealed that fear of death is not just a philosophical issue. It has been shown that death anxiety is a basic fear underlying various mental health conditions, such as hypochondriasis (excessive worries about illnesses), panic disorder, and anxiety and depressive disorders.[1]

Existential death anxiety has raised questions among scholars throughout history: Do we have the right to bring children into this world without their consent, knowing that they will inevitably face death? Regardless of entering into discussions about these philosophical issues, it is clear that humans have always been concerned with death and their responsibility for the deaths of their loved descendants. The book Better Never to Have Been: The Harm of Coming Into Existence by David Benatar is one of the best-known contemporary works on antinatalism (the belief that having children is unjustifiable).[3]

To avoid philosophical debates about the meaning of life and falling into nihilism, this perspective focuses on the rights of patients with serious and painful diseases. Although everyone faces inevitable death sooner or later, these patients have a unique situation: They may be aware that death is near, while healthy people can more easily keep thoughts of their own mortality at a distance.

The duality of continuing life with suffering and intentional ending of a person's life

In patients with life-threatening illnesses, anxiety becomes more complex as it mixes with pain, suffering, loss of independence, and concerns about the meaning of life, leading to the need for psychological interventions. Various studies have proposed that psychological methods—for instance, methods based on terror management theory (TMT)—can help patients understand how to confront death and make end-of-life decisions.[2] According to TMT, the awareness of the inevitability of death can create anxiety that humans manage by relying on cultural beliefs, religious beliefs, a sense of personal worth, and meaningful relationships.

article continues after advertisement

With the legalization of euthanasia in France, ethical and sociological debates surrounding the issue have been reignited. Euthanasia and physician-assisted suicide are practices that raise questions about the rights of people experiencing severe suffering due to serious or incurable illness. Now, few countries accept this right legally, including the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, Canada, and, recently, France. The word "euthanasia" comes from the Greek roots "eu," meaning good, and "thanatos," meaning death. Commonly, euthanasia is a physician-assisted active procedure, and doctors administer medications that provide an easy death. However, there is a type of euthanasia in which someone may refuse treatment and choose death passively.

In some cultures, particularly in religious societies, euthanasia is forbidden. In most religions, human life is considered sacred. Therefore, challenges around the right to end suffering from disease continue to persist. Some believe that acceptance of euthanasia may open the way for the legalization of suicide because the logic behind it is the same.

However, is there another ethical way to rescue patients from pain without helping to kill them? One might envision a third scenario: a profound alteration of subjective experience in which the individual remains alive, yet their relationship to pain, fear, personal identity, and even their sense of "self" is transformed.

Modern medicine can help terminally ill patients to die peacefully

Modern medicine offers options to reduce suffering at the end of life without necessarily ending a patient's life.

A new systematic review examined psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy, including psilocybin and LSD, for anxiety, depression, and existential distress in people with life-threatening diseases.[4] However, further research is needed to clarify the efficacy, safety, and appropriate use of classical psychedelics in these patients, as they may also cause anxiety, psychological agitation, and increases in blood pressure and heart rate.[5]

But approved medical options already exist. Palliative sedation is used in clinical practice for patients with advanced disease whose symptoms cannot be relieved by other means. Sedatives such as midazolam and lorazepam reduce the patient’s level of consciousness, and guidelines recommend their use only as a proportionate, carefully monitored response to refractory suffering.[6]

article continues after advertisement

The question arises: Why—perhaps due to economic reasons or a lack of cost-benefit analysis—do governments and healthcare systems leave patients and their anxious loved ones to face death alone? Perhaps the right to a peaceful death, free from terror, is a more ethical issue than the broader debate surrounding the right to end one's life.

item.title: Anxiety: The Overlooked Stage of Grief
item.description:
Grief

Anxiety: The Overlooked Stage of Grief

Anxiety and grief are strongly associated and widely experienced together.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows a strong correlation between grief and anxiety, rumination, fixation, and hypervigilance.
  • Traditional models of the grieving process can be broadened to include additional responses such as anxiety.
  • Common anxiety responses to grief include fear to further loss, health anxiety, and loss of safety.

You have heard them before—at this point, they have become part of the parlance of grief and loss—denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. These “five stages of grief,” introduced by Elisabeth Kübler-Ross in her 1969 book, On Death and Dying, are widely accepted and understood as common to the emotional process that follows the death of a loved one. While there have been additions and suggestions to Kübler-Ross’ original model over time, most notably by David Kessler, one of her students, who suggested that “finding meaning” be added to the process, the main tenets of the model remain resonant and relevant today. Even so, grief is more complex than this classic model illustrates. It can include a plethora of emotions that can occur alongside the five that have been popularized over the years.

One of these other emotions that falls within the common feelings associated with grief and loss is anxiety. A 2012 article in Current Psychiatry Reports concludes that “anxiety is a natural response of the attachment system to separation from a loved one … Confrontation with one’s own death is also a natural trigger of anxiety … [and] loss of a loved one can trigger the onset of a [diagnosable] anxiety disorder that, when present, can derail the mourning process and prolong acute grief” (Shear et al., 2012).

Essentially, loss causes us to feel a sense of abandonment, thoughts of our own mortality, and symptoms associated with anxiety disorders, all of which can be commonly found in an individual’s emotional response to loss and can complicate the widely accepted “framework” of the grieving process.

Loss of Safety

Anxiety thrives on perception of threat; in other words, the more we believe we are at risk, the more anxiety we feel. While the death of a loved one is not necessarily a direct or tangible threat to our own safety, it can trigger intense feelings of worry and uncertainty. Unexpected or traumatic deaths can shatter an individual’s sense of safety and predictability.

A 2016 study found that symptoms of anxiety were strongly associated with prolonged grief (Eisma et al., 2016). Furthermore, personalization of the loss (turning our thoughts towards our own mortality) is common and can bring about a sense of vulnerability and worry.

In some cases, this loss of safety can exhibit as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which has been shown to be statistically significant as related to the death of a close loved one (Buur et al., 2025). PTSD is strongly associated with anxiety and can cause anxious responses such as intrusive thoughts, rumination, panic-like physical symptoms, hypervigilance, and sleep disturbance (National Center for PTSD, 2023). The loss of safety and certainty that often accompany loss is a common cause of grief-related anxiety.

Health Anxiety

When the loss of a loved one is the result of a traumatic or prolonged illness such as cancer, it is not uncommon for survivors, and particularly caregivers, to experience health-related anxiety.

In my 2023 book, Understanding and Coping with Illness Anxiety, I discuss this phenomenon: “Those who care for sick family members may be more prone to illness-related anxiety based upon the sheer proximity to illness and the personalized nature of caring for a closely related individual … [this] comes with its own trauma: a constant exposure to disease and sickness, as well as a need to always be vigilant for health changes, emergencies, or urgent situations” (Lane, 2023).

article continues after advertisement

Continued or long-term exposure to unpleasant or frightening stimuli can cause us to experience heightened anxiety and worry and, in the case of health anxiety, the closeness to illness can trigger worries about our own physical health status. Not only is the bereaved person coping with the actual loss, but they are also coping with complicated feelings about their own health based upon the continued negative stimulus of caregiving.

Fear of Further Loss

When a traumatic event occurs, a common emotional response is hypervigilance, which we might summarize as “self-preservation.” Basically, in an effort not to re-experience the traumatic event, we become hyperaware of possible threats. This can look like rumination, fixation, and a general sense of being on “high alert.”

In her book, Trauma and Recovery, Judith Herman writes, “After a traumatic experience, the human system of self-preservation seems to go onto a permanent alert, as if the danger might return at any moment” (Herman, 1992).

Existing in this state of high alert, while seemingly protecting us from future danger, can actually cause us to experience disruptive anxiety and struggle to feel present in our lives. Though experiencing a loss can be shocking, it does not predict that more loss is about to occur—but the anxious mind struggles to make this distinction, and we can become fixated on the possibility of an additional loss.

An Evolving Framework

The human experience of grief has an evolutionary component to it; rather than being a phenomenon we can rigidly describe, grief has a certain nebulousness about it which allows us to continually broaden our understanding of the experience. Kübler-Ross’ work helped us formulate an initial psychological understanding of emotional processes related to grief and loss while also leaving space for further exploration and depth. As we continue to broaden our understanding of the psychology of grief, we must recognize the role that anxiety plays in what is a complicated and nonlinear process.

item.title: Mental Gymnastics: How to Handle Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

Mental Gymnastics: How to Handle Anxiety

When we we can’t stop preparing, we actually make it harder to succeed.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Mental Gymnastics refers to the act of doing a lot of thinking, often about complex and complicated topics.
  • Thinking about anxiety as Mental Gymnastics can help externalize it and make it easier to see the cycle.
  • Mindfulness is the antidote to anxiety; it takes trial and error to find what activities work best for you.

This post is about anxiety, which is something we all experience at some point in our lives to different degrees. Anxiety is characterized by an unpleasant state of inner turmoil and includes feelings of dread over anticipated events. Much of my work with clients experiencing anxiety involves, on one hand, an examination of the possible outcomes of anticipated events, and on the other hand, the physical and emotional ways the inner turmoil that the anticipation of these events can cause.

Runaway Thoughts

Anxiety can be characterized by runaway thoughts. You just can’t stop thinking about anticipated events, and the idea that they could go badly causes this inner turmoil. In session, a client might list several different ways things could go bad at the big work event tomorrow. It’s my job as a therapist to avoid getting into a back-and-forth about these thoughts. Friends and loved ones might react to this kind of discussion with words of encouragement, rebutting the client’s negative thoughts with positive ones, listing reasons why things will actually go well. Of course, this never makes the client feel better, and any suggestions toward the positive are often parried away with negative reactions that lead us right back to the place we started, deep down in the pit of anxiety. As a therapist, it’s not my job to come up with reasons to be excited or positive or not anxious. I’m here to explore the feelings of anxiety, not so much specifically in terms of how the work event will go this week, but more in the acceptance that this anxiety exists. We can only learn to work with it, to accept it, to understand it, and in the process lessen its power to keep us up at night.

But keep us up at night it does! Clients with moderate to intense anxiety might report being unable to sleep because they can’t stop thinking about some event in the future that will certainly go wrong. This is an example of what we might call Mental Gymnastics. It’s a common term that refers to the act of doing a lot of thinking, often about complex and complicated topics. It’s as if our client is a gymnast with a big meet coming up, but they are so anxious about their upcoming performance that they stay in the gym working on their routine over and over and over again. They work on this routine so much that eventually they become exhausted, and by the time the day of the meet comes around, they’re so sick of gymnastics that what was once an enjoyable and pleasant activity is now a slog, something to just get over with so we can be done with it.

What’s the best way for a gymnast to prepare for a meet? Now, I am not a gymnast, have never been to a gymnastics meet, and cannot do a cartwheel. But I asked around, and the general consensus seems to be practice and preparation, of course, but not so much that the gymnast is exhausted by the day of the meet. There is a certain amount of rest needed, both physical and mental. You practice all you can, prepare your best, and then rest up for the actual competition. By being so concerned about being prepared that we can’t stop preparing, we’re actually making it harder for us to succeed.

article continues after advertisement

Coping With Anxiety

Hopefully the client will be able to see themselves as this gymnast, spending so much time worrying about the outcome of an event that they are in fact making it more likely that it will turn out just as badly as they imagine. Of course, this doesn’t make it any easier to stop an anxiety-fueled night of tossing and turning. But it might help us realize how not just futile but ultimately counterproductive our anxiety patterns are. Here is where we will then talk about the many ways to cope with anxiety. Not eliminate it, or bypass it, or zap it away, but cope, meaning to reduce. What can we do to reduce this stress and anxiety? This includes all the classics, like meditation, exercise, listening to music, etc. In session with clients, we’ll drill down into coping skills more specific to them, like going for a walk, listening to classical music, or cleaning the kitchen. Mindfulness is the antidote to anxiety, but it takes trial and error to figure out what activities work best for you.

It’s not the idea that we’re wasting all our energy as Mental Gymnasts the night before the big meet that somehow makes the anxiety go away. Thinking about it in this way can help externalize it, though, and in this way make it easier to see the cycle you are caught in as opposed to feeling like you’re inside the washing machine. From there, finding the right coping skills can help to reduce the anxiety until you reach a point where the anxiety hits, you identify it, and then know you can cope with it, reducing its effects to the point where it no longer keeps you up at night.

item.title: Helping Traumatized Children With Severe Behaviors
item.description:
Parenting

Helping Traumatized Children With Severe Behaviors

These tips can help when troubled children push your buttons.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Unresolved fear drives severe behavior in traumatized children.
  • Severe behavior, in turn, can trigger unresolved fear in parents.
  • Awareness and skills can benefit children and parents alike—whether adoptive, foster, or biologic parents.
Source: Nesho / istockphoto

Children who've experienced adversity, especially in the earliest months and years of life, often manifest troubling behaviors arising from their pain—including rage and aggression against adoptive parents (especially the mother), defiance, and shunning of parental affection. Many well-meaning adoptive parents are shocked to find that their children can trigger strong feelings of rage and inadequacy. The dynamics of adoptive relationships reveal insights that might benefit many other parents.

In a study by Forbes and Dziegielewski of adoptive mothers of children with special needs—mothers who were distressed enough to seek therapy—77 percent indicated that since adopting, they experienced more rage and anger than ever before. Many mothers were shocked to feel desires to seriously hurt their children or themselves. Many mothers reported stress-related physical and mental health problems, exhaustion, changes in self-image, and marital strains.

In Beyond Consequences, Logic, and Control, authors Forbes and Post offer helpful tips. They explain that children’s severe behaviors, as well as parents’ strong reactions to the behaviors, spring from strong, unresolved fears. When stress and emotions are beyond the window of tolerance, the general guidelines are to first calm the parent and child until the brain’s reasoning regions re-engage, connect with the child, and then correct.

Don’t Fear Your Past—or Your Pain

The unnerving behaviors of troubled children can stir memories of our own inadequacy or shame—dark places we weren’t consciously aware of, places that we protect with anger. These old troubling memories, once activated, can be changed by the brain. In this way, troubled children can be a gift that leads us to address the buried pain and resolve it. Once resolved, we no longer need our anger to protect against the pain.

One child’s defiance stirred rage and feelings of inadequacy in the parent. Skilled therapy and introspection helped her to realize the origin of those feelings—feeling ineffective to stop her parents’ divorce, her inability to lift her mother’s depression, and her own feelings of rejection. After processing these difficult memories, she was then able to take a deep breath, know that the child’s pain need not trigger her own, and focus on how to help the misbehaving child, not hurt her.

When a Child Lies, Acknowledge Their Fear

The authors indicate that liars include unfaithful spouses, con artists, criminals, and others who hurt people. Perhaps some parents have an overly stern reaction to their child’s lying because they themselves were lied to when young. Perhaps they fear that lying will ruin their child’s life.

article continues after advertisement

For traumatized children, lying is a life-or-death survival strategy to protect against abandonment or rejection (e.g., “If I admit my flaws—if I’m imperfect—I’ll be unloved, punished, or sent away.”). Punishment doesn’t allay the child’s fear.

When a child lies, parents can first calm themselves, and then perhaps give the child a hug and reassure them. Later, when both are regulated, parents can address the importance of telling the truth—how lying damages trust and hurts people. Explain: “Sometimes we lie when we are scared. You are safe here. You can tell me if you made a mistake and I’ll help you.”

Soothe the Internal Distress Behind Compulsive Stealing

The authors suggest viewing stealing as an addiction that soothes internal dysregulation for a brief period of time—calming the hyper-aroused child and giving a rush of alertness for the hypo-aroused child. But like other addictions, the stealing child continues to need another “fix” after the short-lived regulation wears off.

The authors suggest a discussion when both are calm: “When stressed and scared, it feels good to stick something in your pocket. When you feel that way, come to me. Taking things that don’t belong to you hurts and scares people and makes them angry.”

The parent might practice walking into Walmart, keeping the child closer to feel safe, walking up and down the aisles, and returning home, perhaps to a treat. Encourage teachers to say: “I know when you get stressed and scared in class, you feel like stealing from my desk. I want you to know that everything is going to be all right and I’m here to help you. The next time you feel like putting something in your pocket, raise your hand and ask me to come to your desk. You won’t be punished. You have someone to share your feelings with. So please let me help you.”

Demonstrate Food Security to Relieve Hoarding and Gorging

Children who were deprived of food and had no parent to comfort them emotionally often learned to soothe themselves with food hidden in their rooms.

The parent might say, “I know when you get stressed out, you feel the urge to eat something sweet to feel calmer. If you wake up in the middle of the night and need a hug, come wake me up. It’s okay if you are scared and stressed. I’ll sit with you.”

article continues after advertisement

The parent might give the child a snack, and during the day, allow the child to have healthy snacks in a fanny pack to reassure them that food is available.

De-escalate Before Addressing Aggression

The overactive amygdala reacts to perceived threats in a millisecond. The contentedly playing traumatized child who is accidentally bumped might aggressively turn on another child in terror. Even a parent’s angry reaction might elicit biting, kicking, spitting, hitting—survival responses learned early in life. The parent might say, “You look so scared. Come sit with me, dear. You are safe. No one will hurt you. I’m going to keep you safe.” Later on, discuss that hitting and hurting others is wrong.

For the child who throws a tantrum when told to turn off the TV for dinner, the parent might sit beside the child and say, “Dear, in 10 minutes we’re going to have to turn off the TV for dinner.” Five minutes later, the instruction is repeated to prepare the child for a calm transition.

A teen explodes upon returning from school. When his father asks about his day, he yells, “It was terrible. What do you care?” The father calmly says, “I’ll be in the office. Let me know if you need me.” Later, the father goes to the boy’s room and says: “How about saying respectfully, ‘I had a bad day,’ and we talk about it if you like?”

Other Tips

Among the other tips are:

  • Don’t demand eye contact when you are angry. This can further scare the already fearful child and trigger defiance or a glazed look.
  • Prepare the child who acts up when taken to the store. Explain: “Leaving home and going to the store can be scary. I’ll stay close to keep you safe.” Practice going there for a very short time, and come home quickly, perhaps to a game or snack.
  • If the child resists homework and can’t concentrate, ask why homework is scary. Listen. Remind them that homework is important, but they are more important than their grades.

item.title: Boredom Is Uncomfortable; That May Be the Point
item.description:
Boredom

Boredom Is Uncomfortable; That May Be the Point

What children may learn when we resist the urge to entertain them.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Boredom can be a state or a trait.
  • Boredom is something that most people generally find unpleasant.
  • Boredom can potentially help children develop self-regulation and coping strategies.

Every parent knows the phrase. If you’re lucky, you might only hear it once in a while. But for some of us, it’s something that can be heard weekly, if not daily. My kids have had days where there’s a sports game in the morning, a birthday party in the afternoon, an impromptu friend hang, dinner together, and then a movie, and as soon as the living room is cleared of friends, one of them will inevitably say it….Mom, I’m bored.

A State or a Trait

Boredom is something we’ve all experienced. Boredom is a state of feeling restless or uninspired because something about your current situation lacks stimulation, challenge, or meaning. At least that’s what the internet says. Scientists think of boredom in a bit more complicated way (as scientists usually do). According to psychologists, boredom can be a state—which is something about the current situation you’re in. But it can also be a trait, something about your personality, or how susceptible you are to feeling bored, with some people feeling boredom easily, and others feeling boredom more rarely. Either way, boredom is something that most people generally find unpleasant. So unpleasant that people will do some crazy things to avoid it.

In one classic set of studies, researchers asked college students to spend 6 to 15 minutes in a room by themselves with nothing to do. They were told to entertain themselves with their thoughts, and the only rules were to stay seated and awake. As you can imagine, young adults didn’t like this very much. In fact, in one version of the study, they were given the option to administer a mild but unpleasant electric shock to themselves while they were just sitting there as a break from their own thoughts. Note, the electric shock was unpleasant enough that people were willing to actually pay money to avoid it. But when given the option to shock themselves or simply be left alone with their thoughts, 25 percent of women and a whopping 67 percent of men chose the shock (Wilson et al., 2014). You read that correctly: Many of these college students would rather give themselves electric shocks than face boredom. That’s some intense dislike.

Is Boredom Harmful?

My question (and the question on lots of parents' minds) is whether boredom is actually a bad thing, especially for our kids. Sure, being bored is well—boring—but is it harmful?

It turns out that the kind of boredom that is associated with personality—trait boredom—isn’t great. It can reduce our motivation to do things; it can lead to financial risk-taking and unhealthy eating and substance use. It’s also associated with depression and anxiety (Perone et al., 2026). This probably rings true for a lot of us. When I’m bored, I shop online, and I eat Taco Bell. It’s no wonder that boredom is associated with financial risk-taking and unhealthy eating.

But what about state boredom? The research on this is a little fuzzier, but there is some evidence that experiencing boredom helps kids learn how to deal with being bored, which could be a very positive thing. In one study, researchers asked 4- to 6-year-old children and their parents about what it’s like to be bored, and then actually gave kids a boring task to complete. Some parents were more likely to intervene when they heard that inevitable “I’m bored, mom!” while others were more likely to let their kids figure it out for themselves. Importantly, the parents who let their kids figure out how to resolve their own boredom showed activity in the brain associated with approach when given a boring task to do. This suggests that the kids who were left to deal with boredom on their own were more likely to cope with it proactively than the kids whose parents were more likely to intervene (Perone et al., 2026). Indeed, when kids are left on their own to deal with boredom, they tend to come up with activities to occupy their time. As a result, the authors concluded that boredom can potentially help children develop self-regulation and coping strategies (Anderson & Perone, 2024).

article continues after advertisement

So should we intervene when our children are bored? The answer is not necessarily. Giving them a little bit of space to generate their own solutions to boredom is a great first step, as it could help them build coping strategies to deal with boredom on their own. If they have trouble, you could help them by scaffolding some potential solutions. So instead of saying “Here’s what you could do,” maybe ask them, “What are a few things you might want to do?” and then help them generate some ideas from there. The idea isn’t necessarily to help prevent boredom, but to help them learn how to tolerate the unpleasantness of being bored and to figure out some solutions on their own. This will hopefully help them cope with feelings that are unpleasant, and maybe even build some creativity in the process.

item.title: Is Eating Animals a Psychological Blind Spot?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Is Eating Animals a Psychological Blind Spot?

A new wave of psychologists is exposing the invisible mentality of meat eating.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Most of us never wonder why we eat some animals but not others, and that's no accident.
  • A fast-growing field studying the psychology of eating animals is catalyzing change among psychologists.
  • Research shows we justify eating animals with the "three Ns:" it's normal, natural, and necessary.

Throughout history, psychologists have played a critical role in both enabling and challenging injustice. For example, in 1912, psychologist Henry Goddard claimed that social problems were rooted in inherited low intelligence, helping to justify the forced sterilization of tens of thousands of people deemed "unfit" to have children. Later, in 1973, psychologists' research helped lead to the declassification of homosexuality as a mental illness.

Today, psychologists are again challenging harmful norms, this time those that sustain one of the most entrenched institutions: big animal agriculture. Apart from being a leading driver of climate change, public health crises, and human rights abuses, animal agriculture is responsible for the slaughter of more animals in a single day than the total number of people killed in all wars throughout history. A key reason this industry persists is that the invisible mentality that drives it is as entrenched as the industry itself.

Carnism and the Carnistic Mentality

Since my book Why We Love Dogs, Eat Pigs, and Wear Cows was published in 2010, an entire research field has emerged. My early research had led me to identify what I call carnism, the invisible belief system that conditions people to eat certain animals. Carnism is sustained by a problematic mentality, which has flown under the radar of most psychologists because it's so normal it seems unremarkable.

The "carnistic mentality" exists because humans are naturally inclined to feel empathy for others, including animals, and most of us are opposed to animals being subjected to needless suffering. Yet most of us also eat animals—not because we need to, but because we've always eaten animals and because we like how they taste. The result is cognitive dissonance, which we manage with unconscious psychological strategies, or "carnistic defenses," constituting the carnistic mentality. Carnistic defenses hide the contradictions between our values and behaviors, so that we unknowingly make exceptions to what we would normally consider unethical.

Consider the following scenario: You're biting into a juicy hamburger when your dining companion tells you that the meat is actually made from a golden retriever. Chances are, what you'd just perceived as food you now see as a dead animal; what you'd felt was delicious, you now feel is disgusting; so rather than continue to eat the burger, you probably throw it away and maybe even want to take to the streets in protest. If you were Hindu, you'd likely feel the same way about a beef burger. In meat-eating cultures around the world, people learn to classify a small handful of animals as edible and find the idea of eating others disgusting and often unthinkable. And although the type of animal consumed changes from culture to culture, the carnistic mentality remains consistent.

Carnistic defenses are distancing mechanisms; they disconnect us from our authentic thoughts and feelings when it comes to so-called edible animals. For example, carnism has conditioned us to view farmed animals as objects (we refer to the chicken on our plate as something, rather than someone) and as abstractions, lacking any individuality or personality of their own (we assume that a pig is a pig and all pigs are the same), and to create rigid categories in our minds so that we can harbor different feelings and carry out very different behaviors toward different species (cows are for eating and dogs are our friends).

article continues after advertisement

Institutionalized Beliefs and Behaviors

Carnism is institutionalized. For example, when we study nutrition, we actually study carnistic nutrition. Carnistic institutions teach us to believe that eating animals is normal, natural, and necessary—the three* Ns of justification. Perhaps not surprisingly, these same arguments have been used to justify other harmful systems, such as racism and patriarchy.

Carnism is structured like other systems that are built on prejudice. Although the experience of each set of victims is unique, the mentality that enables the harm is the same. When we take part in one form of prejudice, we may strengthen the mentality that sustains all the others.

Of course, most of us know that the thinking that reflects and reinforces prejudice—such as othering and instrumentalizing—is harmful. And we recognize harming animals (e.g., companion animal abuse) as a psychological red flag. Yet we may ignore or even celebrate the very same kind of thinking when it comes to how we relate to the animals we've learned to classify as edible, and misconstrue thinking that defies it. We may, for example, assume that a young woman's decision to stop eating animals is indicative of an eating disorder, rather than of an emotionally mature choice to live in greater alignment with her values.

Challenging Entrenched Assumptions and Norms

Many researchers are now examining how and why we eat animals. The psychological study of eating animals has become a recognized subfield, complete with a scientific society—the Society for the Psychology of Human-Animal Intergroup Relations (PHAIR)—a peer-reviewed journal, and a biennial international conference. Researchers have published thousands of papers and developed multiple validated psychometric tools, including scales measuring carnism and the three Ns of justification, to study what has become known as the "meat paradox." The field has also produced academic anthologies and popular books.

I'm proud to be part of a profession willing to challenge deeply entrenched assumptions about what's normal and healthful, and to help cultivate a better world for everyone.

item.title: The Impact of AI on Who We Are and Who We Become
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Impact of AI on Who We Are and Who We Become

We need to become more conscious users rather than merely passive consumers of AI.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • AI systems map our preferences, patterns, and choices and influence them, too, creating an “algorithmic self."
  • The algorithmic self shapes the human psyche without us even realising.
  • Gen Z are the most active and conscious users of AI.

This post is Part 1 of a series.

I’m currently reading a fascinating book about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on human intimacy,1 which I heard about during the last training event I attended, which was about AI and the psyche. The last three media requests I’ve received were for comments about various aspects of young people’s use of AI, or AI as a substitute for a human therapist. The most recent presentation I delivered was about adolescent identity in the age of AI, and next I’ll be speaking on a panel about the same. Many of the threads on my social media feed are about AI, too—people loving and learning about it or vehemently rallying against it and arguing that it’s not for them.

So, why is everybody talking about AI?

AI is not new; it’s older than me and older than many of you. The first use of the term “artificial intelligence” can be traced back to the 1950s, when Alan Turing asked people to spot the difference between machine and human intelligence. But it really came to the fore with the launch of ChatGPT in 2022. Gen Alpha, the first of whom were born in 2010, are the first generation to be “AI-natives,” but it’s Gen Z, born a decade earlier, who are the most active and conscious users of AI.

How Gen Z Interacts With AI

Gen Z do things differently from older generations. They’re more likely to “AI it” rather than “Google it,” using long, highly contextual, goal-based queries instead of keywords to help with personal and work-related cognitive tasks. They are more likely than older generations to turn to AI to offload relationship dilemmas, too. Many (about 75 percent) use AI as emotional, social, and sexual companions. According to one study, almost half of Gen Z users have formed a “meaningful relationship” with an AI companion and a quarter believe it could replace a human partner.2 Gen Z are also using AI to search for, and in some cases substitute for, a therapist.

I’ll bet you’re using AI, too, but probably not so intentionally as your Gen Z contemporaries. You’re using it to track your way from A to B with apps like Google Maps and Waze. You’re using it to binge-watch that box set on Netflix, and it’s why you receive notifications such as: “Because you watched that, we think you might like this.” Ditto Spotify. Ditto YouTube. You hovered over one funny cat video, and now you’re inundated with them? AI did that. Every online shopping platform you’ve opened has tracked your browsing history so it can tempt you about what to buy next, which is also feeding the algorithm that influences your social media feed. You asked Alexa or Siri or Claude about the weather in Brazil and Googled how to keep your aspidistra alive, and now exotic holidays and houseplants are popping up all over every app you open. That’s no coincidence; that’s AI.

How AI Shapes Preferences, Behaviors, and the 'Algorithmic Self'

AI systems map our preferences, patterns, and choices, and they influence them, too, creating a sort of “algorithmic self.” Offloading memory, attention, and decision-making to AI risks flattening individuality and reducing authentic self-expression. Tools like mood-trackers, personalised feeds, and AI assistants shape how we understand our internal emotional landscapes and shape our behaviour. Am I buying another personalised keepsake because of sentimentality or because AI has seduced me into it? Do I feel emotionally depleted on certain days because of hormone fluctuations or because my AI mood tracker told me I would?

article continues after advertisement

The worry is that the “algorithmic self” shapes the human psyche without us even realising, and that reliance on AI during adolescence, when the self hasn’t yet fully developed, could even pose a threat to individuation. Development of the self relies heavily on friction, trial and error, and navigating the unknown. By replacing these struggles with optimised, predictable convenience, AI risks turning active self-discovery into passive consumption. It therefore challenges the very concept of “self” by shifting human identity from an internal creation to a data-driven one.

Does this mean AI is bad? I don’t think so. But I do think we need to become more conscious users rather than merely passive consumers. And I think we need to remember that every search, scroll, view, listen, chat, and journey becomes data that will shape what we do next. Hopefully AI will lead you back here, to my next blog post, where I’m sure I’ll be talking about AI some more.

item.title: The Lost Art of Not Knowing
item.description:
Infidelity

The Lost Art of Not Knowing

Are we cheating ourselves out of wonder?

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • At a time when information was not so accessible, perhaps it was more common to wonder.
  • Accepting that we can't or don't know some things is difficult in the digital age.
  • By not exercising skill of reason, we make ourselves more vulnerable to manipulation.

My partner James (pictured here in his natural habitat) is the inspiration for this post. During a night of trivia, as we observed other teams looking up answers after each round, he made a comment to me: "People don't not know much anymore." He talked to me about the lost art of not knowing, and he was right.

Source: Jennifer Gerlach

In our current age, it's impossible to get away from information. We spend less time wondering.

Driving, even on routes I could guess myself, I turn on the navigation. My chances of getting caught up in a newly forming traffic jam are sliced, but so are my chances of wandering around a bit.

Sometimes it feels good to get a bit lost.

Don't know, can't know

The information superhighways have grown enormously in the last few years. What in the past we'd have no way to know except maybe by going to a library (and hoping the book we were handling had accurate, up-to-date information) or asking someone (and hoping they were telling the truth), we can look up without thought.

Yet, it could be asked if it has taken away from us some sense of wonder or inclination to seek answers in our own ways.

Watching a reel recently (I know), I saw a man purporting that if you ask a chatbot to ask you 10 questions about yourself that even you can't answer, that you won't need a therapist anymore. Tongue-in-cheek, of course. Still, he highlighted a very real phenomenon that I have observed recently; namely people turning to technology, especially AI chatbots, in an attempt to know things that can't really be known.

In a sense, when we hand over this process to machines, they become spiritual in nature.

I worry how this may limit people's natural paths towards discovery and self-understanding.

This concerns me especially as curiosity is one of the most robustly studied ingredients to a rainbow of aspects of well-being (Priemysheva et al., 2025), in particular protecting against depression (Priemysheva et al., 2024).

Wonder makes life worthwhile.

Do we understand the difference between facts and opinions?

The truth is, facts are sometimes concrete, but the conclusions we draw from them almost never are. In personal reflection, conversation, life experience, hearing others' stories, and consideration of the facts, we find our way to our own beliefs. Ready access to other people's opinions online makes it easier to shortcut this process into parroting others' ideas as our own.

article continues after advertisement

I have had multiple interactions over the last few years that make me wonder how many people are able to navigate the difference between facts and opinions.

Embracing the subjective nature of ideas is essential to critical thinking. If we pawn off our critical thinking too much to machines, I worry the skill will atrophy.

The virtue of not knowing and 3 things you can do

So, these days I'm driving with navigation turned off a little more and purposely giving myself time to write by hand as I contemplate. Practices like these are returning more opportunity to wander and wonder into my life. I am embracing the virtue of not-knowing, and these are things you can do too.

  1. Check Out New Places. Maybe you are driving and you see a park you've never been to, but it's not on the planned route. If you have time, maybe consider stopping in.
  2. Journal by Hand. Why write by hand when you can type? Because a piece of paper isn't connected to any AI or social media. Intentionally taking time to journal by hand, especially when you notice a reaction of yours and ask a question to bravely look past what you already know, a known process in Radically Open DBT as self-inquiry journaling, especially gives some ability to loosen up on preloaded ideas and be open to discovery (Lynch et al., 2015)
  3. Ask Someone a Story From Their Life. Everyone you know has many stories that you have never heard. Ask about them and listen. This simple practice not only helps us to connect with one another, but it reminds us of how much there is beyond us.

item.title: Lighten Up: Laughter Is Good Medicine
item.description:
Laughter

Lighten Up: Laughter Is Good Medicine

Humor helps focus and mental fitness, and reduces stress.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Laughter provides a clinically significant, non-invasive benefits.
  • Watching humorous content reduces psychological stress and boosts mood.
  • Videos as short as four minutes can produce measurable benefits from laughter.

One of the most rewarding, enjoyable, and affordable pleasures in life is laughter. It relaxes our muscles, calms our mind, and is best enjoyed with others. Yet laughter apparently has additional benefits to both mind and body that are particularly relevant as we age. Research explains.

Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

Laughter Over the Lifespan

Tatsuya Yamakoshi et al. (2025) examined the impact of laughter on stress and focus on middle-aged adults.[i] Studying 25 healthy Japanese-speaking adults aged 40-65, they demonstrated how a short-term laughter-based experiment provided support for the clinically significant, non-invasive benefit of humor.

Yamakoshi et al. showed participants a four-minute video clip, either comedic or a control video, followed by a series of physical and cognitive measures. They found that adults who viewed the humorous video experienced increased parasympathetic activity and a reduction in psychological stress levels, measured by both physical and mental measures. They recognize that laughter is helpful to psychosocial and physical health and has been acknowledged as a method of alleviating depression and anxiety. They explain that laughter reduces stress hormones, activates natural killer cells, which boosts immunity, and lowers blood pressure. Adding to its utility, they note laughter therapy is non-pharmacological, non-invasive, and relatively easy to administer. Accordingly, it is viewed as a good complement to other treatments as a way to lessen the impact of disease and increase the health of middle-aged adults. Considering the nature of the benefits, however, laughter is clearly good medicine for individuals of any age.

Improving Mood and Focus

Yamakoshi et al. found additional laughter-related benefits in their study beyond what had been documented in prior research. Acknowledging the benefit of video-based interventions, they looked at the impact on adults between the ages of 40–65 years, whereas previous studies investigated people over the age of 65. They also note that while prior studies investigated the impact of 20-minute comedic videos, they demonstrated the benefit of viewing clips of only four minutes.

And regarding mood, Yamakoshi et al. found that subjective mood states were significantly higher in almost all areas after participants watched the comedic video as compared to the control video. This corroborates previous studies finding that laughter creates a temporary boost in mood.

Yamakoshi et al. conclude that even a short comedic video clip can potentially increase focused attention and reduce stress, particularly when performing cognitive tasks. It appears that humor-based interventions are enjoyable, practical methods of addressing stress-induced inattentiveness in daily living and improving the mental health and cognitive functions of middle-aged adults.

article continues after advertisement

As a practical matter, the empirically documented benefits of laughter are consistent with anecdotal experience using laughter to calm nerves, break the ice when meeting someone new, facilitate bonding, and be a free way to boost mood. Lighten the mood with a healthy lifestyle, love, and laughter.

item.title: The Benefits of Exploring Spirituality With Hypnosis
item.description:
Spirituality

The Benefits of Exploring Spirituality With Hypnosis

Hypnospirituality can catalyze personal transformation.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Spiritual experiences generally are subjective and cannot be used to define objective truths.
  • The subconscious can be used to explore personally meaningful spiritual questions.
  • Spiritual imagery or prayer can be used during hypnosis.
Source: Triff/Shutterstock

Hypnospirituality can be described as using the hypnotic state to explore or transform a person's spiritual beliefs, experiences, and sense of connection to something greater than the self.

Traditional therapy with hypnosis generally aims at outcomes such as coping better with mental health issues, improving management of pain or other physical symptoms, or modifying unwanted behaviors. Hypnospirituality helps recognize a spiritual dimension, including:

  • Exploring a person's sense of connection with God or the sacred
  • Using spiritual imagery or prayer during hypnosis
  • Exploring existential questions about meaning and purpose
  • Helping someone experience forgiveness, compassion, gratitude, or acceptance
  • Using the subconscious as a means of exploring personally meaningful spiritual questions
  • Helping patients draw upon spiritual resources that they already consider authentic

Since spiritual experiences generally are subjective in nature, they cannot be used to scientifically define objective truths, such as about the nature of supernatural phenomena. Nonetheless, as I discussed in a previous post, clinicians can validate a patient’s experience without needing to confirm its veracity.

Spiritual material often comes up during my interactions with patients, perhaps because I am open to helping patients work through their spiritual experiences. I have written several blog posts in Psychology Today about such patients, including:

  • An 11-year-old boy who explored his transcendent thoughts with hypnosis
  • A 12-year-old girl who interacted with a ghost
  • A 13-year-old girl who interacted with the serpent from the Garden of Eden
  • A 14-year-old boy who interacted with a demon
  • A 20-year-old woman whose subconscious showed her a life-changing vision of the universe
  • A 25-year-old man who explored the meaning of the universe after a THC-induced psychotic break

Here is an additional story illustrating hypnospirituality from my patient files:

A Lost Murderer

Eli, one of my 15-year-old patients, was so good at not remembering what his subconscious thought that his conscious and subconscious used to play poker with each other.

One day, Eli asked me, “Can someone have two subconsciouses?”

article continues after advertisement

“I don’t think so,” I replied.

“I think another subconscious came into me last night,” he said.

“Why do you say that?”

“I hear him, and I know what he’s thinking.”

“What is that?”

“He is a criminal who used to work for Stalin. He murdered lots of people. He’s looking for his family, but he can’t find them. So, he came into me.”

Eli didn’t look particularly distressed by this supposed invasion, but I did not like the sound of it at all. We needed to deal with this.

I improvised, “It seems to me that we need to get that subconscious to leave you.”

“Yeah, maybe,” he said. “I don’t really want him around.”

“I have an idea,” I said. “Let’s sit on the floor.”

We sat cross-legged across from one another.

“Now, let’s chant,” I said, and I led Eli, who is Jewish like me, in a Jewish kaddish prayer that praises God.

He who makes peace in his high holy places, the prayer concludes, may He bring peace upon us.

“Now,” I said, “let’s invite the criminal’s family to come from the heavens so that they can retrieve him.”

We recited the kaddish again, and I asked Eli to let me know when the family arrived.

A few moments later, he nodded.

“Now,” I said, “let him go.” I showed him how to raise his arms to do so.

Eli raised his arms above him, palms open and fingers splayed toward the sky.

And that was it. He no longer heard his second subconscious.

A metaphorical explanation for this encounter could be that Eli was working out how he could let go of hatred he harbored toward someone he felt had wronged him.

Or, perhaps, he really had become, briefly, a vessel for the soul of a bad man.

A Possible Origin of Spiritual Experiences

In all the aforementioned cases, the patients or their subconscious spontaneously reported their spiritual experiences rather than being prompted by a question I might have posed. The common feature among them is that they had learned how to allow their subconscious to express itself through their therapy.

article continues after advertisement

These patients’ propensity to report spiritual experiences may be related to their concept of the subconscious relationship with the soul and higher powers.

When I have asked patients’ subconscious about this relationship, they generally responded that either they are the soul or deeply connected to it. Some said their soul regularly communes with God, describing God as the living network that connects all beings.

The input my patients have given about their subconscious-prompted spiritual experiences brings to mind a quote associated with the Oracle at Delphi: "Bidden or unbidden, God is present." Psychiatrist Carl Jung, who studied the subconscious and its relationship to spiritual experiences in depth, carved the Latin version of this quote above the entrance to his home.

Takeaway

Learning how to interact with the subconscious through hypnosis can open the door to life-changing spiritual experiences.

item.title: Conservation of Human Value
item.description:
Philosophy

Conservation of Human Value

Applying neo-Piagetian theory to moral decision-making under conflict.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Jean Piaget's notion of conservation, typically applied to perceptions, can also be applied to emotions.
  • The emotion of hatred can be described as a failure of emotional conservation.
  • Soldiers who now condemn their past killing of noncombatants can be described as having evolved past hatred.

In Jean Piaget’s body of research on child development, the concept of “conservation” plays an important role. It refers to one’s ability to hold onto a critical but low-salience reality in the face of a high-salience, distorting event. The best example is probably Piaget’s experiment in which a child is shown two balls of clay and is asked to make sure they are exactly equal. Then one ball is transformed into a cigar shape, and the child is asked whether the ball has more clay, the cigar has more clay, or whether they are both the same. Until around age 5 or 6, a child will say the ball has more (because it is fatter) or the cigar has more (because it is longer), but typically not say that they are the same. Around age 6, when children reach the stage of “concrete operations,” they will say “the same.” They know that the shape looks different, but the mass is the same.

Recently, I watched the British-Israeli documentary Naza, and it occurred to me that hatred can be considered an example of what Piaget called “horizontal décalage.” This occurs when someone who has mastered conservation in one realm (in the case of the two balls, physical) demonstrates a failure to attain conservation in another (in the case of hatred, emotional) realm. The less evolved (in this case, emotional) realm develops later due to it being more complex and less amenable to conscious reflection.

What Is Emotional Non-Conservation and How Does It Cause Hatred?

Emotional non-conservation means that when a person does something terrible, the shock of that action moves them from respect into hatred. Because human beings, in the eyes of mainstream religion (as well as mainstream psychotherapy), never lose their value regardless of their actions, the hatred can be thought of as a failure of emotional conservation.

In Hebrew, naza is an abbreviation for a term meaning “collateral damage.” It was used in the Israeli military in Gaza to estimate the number of noncombatants likely to die when bombing (usually at night) the homes of suspected Hamas operatives. The film consists of interviews with 24 (mostly male) Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers who were involved in developing and operating the AI-driven targeting system used in that process. Thus, if a target was believed to house six non-combatants, it would be described as having “six naza.”

Most of the people anonymously interviewed (such as a drone operator who admits to having killed many noncombatants, including dozens of children) came by 2025 (when the interviews were conducted) to view their actions as morally wrong. When asked why he did what he did, one interviewee said simply “hatred,” pointing to the October 7, 2023 massacre in which approximately 1,200 Israelis (three-fourths of them civilians) were killed. That event was seen as so evil that killing anyone connected to a possible perpetrator was viewed as a justified action. A related aspect of this process, mentioned by some interviewees, is that the targeting system resembled a video game, with all the exhilaration one can feel in obliterating enemy targets not really experienced as actual human beings.

article continues after advertisement

How Does Rational Emotive Therapy Help Overcome Hatred?

In three 2023 Psychology Today posts in which I analyzed the “disappointments, annoyances and hatreds” detailed in Prince Harry’s memoir “Spare,” I alluded to my use of Albert Ellis’ Rational Emotive Therapy (RET) to overcome my own tendency toward emotional dysregulation, including hatred (of self and others). In Ellis’ system, based on both Stoic philosophy and the General Semantics theory of Alfred Korzybski (a former military officer turned pacifist), hatred is a form of over-generalization stemming from use of the verb to be (as in “he is evil”) rather than the verbs to do (as in “he did something undesirable”) or to have (as in “he has some undesirable tendencies”). Emotional maturation in Ellis’ psychotherapy framework (as well as Carl Rogers’ humanistic “Person-Centered Therapy” and its core notion of unconditional positive regard) is grounded in the idea of conserving the value of all humans, no matter what they might have done to us or others.

Moral and emotional evolution away from having hatred as a core motivator is very relevant as well to two of the eight reasons for opposing the death penalty I mentioned in my recent Psychology Today post inspired by the aborted execution of Christa Pike. The two reasons are the moral consensus moving in an abolitionist direction (just under half of American states have abolished it) and the myth that it helps victims’ families to achieve closure. In Europe, where the death penalty has been virtually eliminated (Belarus and Russia are the only countries where it is still on the books, and Russia has had a moratorium on its use since 1996), the main reason cited is Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which states that every human being has a right to life. In terms of victims and their families, it is worth noting that while some families (such as the relatives of the young woman killed by Pike) call for its use, that is not universally the case. As an example, passage of abolitionist legislation in Colorado was made possible when Rhonda Fields, a state senator whose son had been murdered, switched from wanting his killers executed to a different view in which she came to see such a revenge motive as wrong.

Both moral and victim evolution can be seen in the case of the last person executed in the U.S. military: John A. Bennett. He was an African-American soldier hanged in 1961 for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old Austrian girl named Gertrude. Today, when execution in the U.S. is reserved only for the crime of murder, he would be spared for that reason and for his likely having Intellectual Disability. In terms of victim evolution, the morally evolved Gertrude, at age 17, petitioned President Kennedy to spare Bennett’s life, but that request was denied.
