item.title: The Expectations From Porn That Can Ruin Real-Life Intimacy
item.description:
Pornography

The Expectations From Porn That Can Ruin Real-Life Intimacy

Experts break down porn industry tricks and what real intimacy looks like.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Performance myths put unnecessary sexual pressure on couples.
  • Unrealistic body standards can undermine confidence and attraction.
  • There are proven ways to overcome performance anxiety for better sex.
Source: DRT.fm. / Pexels

My early sex education entailed watching Madonna videos and stealing porn mags from under the bed of my best friends’ dad. I wish my parents had simply taught me that an “orgasm” isn’t when you fold paper to look like birds, or that flavored condoms aren’t meant for penetration.

Today, much of what people learn about sex comes from online sources like porn. But entertainment and digital media were never designed to serve as the standard by which real-life intimacy should be measured. Porn also gives young people an unrealistic idea of how quickly a plumber will come to your house.

The Screen vs. the Sheets

Porn versus real life is like pizza rolls from the microwave versus the oven. Pornography looks intensely exciting because it is a heavily produced fantasy designed to exploit human psychology1 and sensory reward systems.

The physical set is highly artificial and profoundly unromantic; it includes a room full of camera operators, a director, lighting technicians, and a boom mic operator. Then post-production editors manipulate the footage for the best sound, angles, color tones, and pacing.

“People should keep in mind that films in general are highly curated, stresses Alicia Rodis, who pioneered the role of intimacy coordinator in the U.S. and currently serves as the in-house intimacy coordinator for HBO.

Though the role of intimacy coordinator is largely absent from the porn industry, the notion of consent is not; it is given through a combination of legal contracts, pre-production discussions, and on-set communication. Actors choose2 which activities they will engage in and with whom.

Performance Myths Create Bedroom Pressure

Because of the grueling, start-and-stop nature of porn shoots, male performers rely on medications like erectile dysfunction drugs to maintain stamina over several hours. Synthetic props, lubricants, and creams are also used on sets to simulate or enhance bodily fluids on camera. The only realism in porn is the “spouse leaving for work.”

In general, most past research3 has focused on the negative outcomes of pornography use, but it has also been associated with more sexual satisfaction4 among partnered women, as well as greater sexual knowledge,5 openness, and excitement. But when a man views pornography, he tends to be not as satisfied6 with his partner’s sexual expression or appearance.

article continues after advertisement

One of the first brain scan studies7 on male pornography users found lower responsiveness to sexual stimulus due to desensitization. Because porn can promote brain changes and subsequent pleasure responses, viewers may eventually feel the need to seek more extreme content. This is what mom meant when she said, “Porn rots your brain.”

Lasting Forever Is Just Movie Magic

UCLA Bioinformatics Programmer Nicole Prause, Ph.D., has found that we have little reliable data on the real length of sexual intercourse. “There are a few ‘stopwatch’ studies where a couple was asked to start a timer on insertion and stop it when sex completed. That period tends to range 3-7 minutes,” she says.

In film and digital media, scenes are spliced together from hours of shooting. A scene that lasts 10 to 15 minutes on screen often takes four or more hours to film, while actors hold contorted, physically exhausting angles.

“Penetration that goes on for extended periods of time can become uncomfortable for the female partner," says Sarah Jones, a clinical psychologist and certified sex therapist. "Once natural or synthetic lubricant starts to dry up, penetration can create friction that leads to microtears and discomfort."

The Truth About Simultaneous Orgasms and Female Pleasure

If porn was accurate, every tryst would end in concurrent orgasms and every woman’s orgasm would be a feat of revelry that might entail screaming epitaphs in the primal language of a lost empire.

The enduring fantasy of the simultaneous orgasm is so pervasive it has become a pinnacle in heterosexual sex. Expecting them every time, however, creates a false standard that leaves both partners feeling like they failed. Media often oversimplifies how satisfaction is achieved, ignoring basic biology and individual preferences.

Unrealistic Body Standards and Visual Expectations

Adult visual media does not objectively mirror reality. Porn prioritizes optics, and its portrayal of idealized, unique bodies and sexual encounters creates a “desire discrepancy."8 In short, things aren’t what they seem. When viewers internalize these hyper-edited visual performances, it often alters how they view both themselves and their partners.

article continues after advertisement

“Pornography has changed remarkably in the last 15 years,” Prause says. “Initially, large production houses selected porn ‘stars’ who tended to have similar features. The resulting data linked pornography viewing to body dissatisfaction,” she says. “Now, OnlyFans and similar democratization of creators means every body type is depicted as sexually arousing to someone."

You Don't Need a Flawless Body or Domination to be Great in Bed

The largest, most in-depth study9 on people who have extraordinary sex, Jones says, identified several qualities that make people great lovers, and none have to do with how one’s body looks: "Rather, they include, amongst other things, being present and attuned with your body, emotional connection with your partner, and open communication."

No one watches porn for complex multiverse storylines. And real chemistry doesn't come from applying a pre-written dynamic; it comes from ongoing dialogue. Dominance without devotion is dysfunction. “Role playing and BDSM are fine options for a couple to explore but when people take on a role that doesn’t genuinely fit them, they’re less able to be authentic or successful in bed,” advises licensed social worker Raffi Bilek.

How to Drop Performance Anxiety for Better Sex

What doesn’t kill you makes you weird at intimacy. Performance anxiety is related to expectations about how we want sex to unfold. “If you are struggling with performance anxiety, talk with your partner about it at a neutral, non-sexual time,” Jones suggests.

You may also benefit from practicing mindfulness10 as this can help you let go of anxiety-related thoughts so you can be present in your body and with your partner. Reality beats fantasy every time. Real intimacy doesn't require perfection; it only requires you to show up, be present, and enjoy the experience together.

article continues after advertisement

“More than anything," Rodis says, "I want people to know they should not model, reflect, or align their intimacy standards based on what they're seeing on their phones, laptops, or screen."

item.title: Childhood Sexual Abuse Can Cause Lasting Damage
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Childhood Sexual Abuse Can Cause Lasting Damage

When teenagers commit violent crimes, there is always a story behind it.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Adverse childhood experiences are often in the background of those who commit violent crimes.
  • Criminal justice system involvement is a significant outcome for people with fetal alcohol syndrome disorder.
  • Child sexual abuse affects a child's neurobiological, physiological, and socio-emotional development.

The case of Christa Pike, now back in prison after surviving a botched execution for the murder of her classmate Colleen Slemmer 30 years ago, raises so many difficult and disturbing questions. Pike was the first woman in the state of Tennessee in 200 years to receive the death sentence.

Beneath all of these events lie the traumatic facts of Pike’s early years. I had interviewed people who had committed violent crimes as teens for my book, Before Their Crimes: What We’re Misunderstanding about Child Trauma, Youth Crime, and the Path to Healing, which made me think about a more specific aspect of the life she had before her crime: sexual abuse that began when she was age 2 and repeated throughout her childhood, up to age 17.

Pike’s seizures during infancy revealed that she had sustained brain damage due to her mother’s alcohol abuse during pregnancy. She was diagnosed with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, FASD, which describes a range of neurodevelopmental deficits that can result from prenatal alcohol exposure. This can affect physical, cognitive, social-emotional, and behavioral functioning. Involvement in the criminal justice system is known to be a significant adverse outcome for many people with FASD (Pei, Flannigan, Keller and colleagues, 2018).

Pike was sexually abused more than once at the age of 2 by a boyfriend of her grandmother. It is impossible to imagine this kind of assault by an adult on a toddler or to fully grasp the catastrophic effect on the developing brain and body of a small child. In Pike’s case, the early sexual assaults and those inflicted on her by other perpetrators at ages 11, 13, and 17 did further harm to a brain already weakened by damage in utero.

Threat Detection and Behavior

Researchers have found that children who have experienced sexual abuse, when compared to their peers who have not been abused, have structural abnormalities in threat detection and response, causing them to be hypervigilant and impulsive, predisposing them to future behavioral problems. These changes may help them adapt to a negative environment in the short term but can lead to future externalization or other psychiatric problems (Demir, Kaya, Ozalay and colleagues, 2023).

The childhoods of many abused children, including Pike, do not include protective, caring adults who are present to prevent further trauma or to help them heal from what has happened to them. Abused children rarely experience safe, loving relationships—ones that reassure them they are valued and worthy.

When their easily triggered sense of danger is aroused, they have few tools to calm themselves or feel safe—even when their alarm system goes off in situations that do not pose a threat. At the same time, they are often repeatedly victimized as a result of their dysregulated stress response; they fail to identify people who may be dangerous.

It isn’t only the brain and body of a sexually abused child that is harmed. The developing sense of self—who I am, what I can expect from others, how they will see and treat me—cannot escape being used as an object by an adult, especially when that adult is a trusted member of the child’s life.

Early Trauma and Aggressive Reactions

In the time since Pike committed her crime, scientific knowledge about brain development and the impact of trauma early in life has exploded. We know that the brain's executive functions—decision-making, judgment, ability to weigh future consequences of our actions—do not fully develop until the late 20s.

article continues after advertisement

We also know that early-occurring stress that is severe or chronic can be said to be “built into our bodies” because it leaves marks on our neurological and psychological stress response systems (Shonkoff and Garner 2012, p. 237). This can lead to highly aggressive reactions in high-pressure moments, especially in the presence of peers.

Advances in scientific knowledge have changed sentencing laws for juvenile offenders. The Supreme Court completely banned the death penalty for people under 18 in 2005, 10 years after Pike’s sentencing, and 28 states have banned juvenile life without parole. In many states, the youth and early circumstances of juvenile offenders, especially their exposures to trauma and maltreatment, are taken into consideration during sentencing.

Pike would likely have received a different sentence had her crime occurred today. At the same time, though we know so much more now than we did then, the great majority of us still have difficulty understanding the harmful nature of child sexual abuse. We need look no further than the example of the Epstein survivors.

In the words of Zeanah and Humphreys, “There may be no single greater environmental predictor of mental health difficulties than experiences of maltreatment.” (2019, p. 3.)

item.title: Indigenous Peoples’ Day vs. Columbus Day
item.description:
Cognition

Indigenous Peoples’ Day vs. Columbus Day

The names we give our holidays influence how we understand the past.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • The names of national holidays affect how societies remember and interpret the past.
  • Language influences whose histories are remembered and whose experiences are overlooked.
  • Renaming a holiday can challenge inherited narratives and broaden historical perspectives.

Every October, the United States marks Columbus Day, a holiday commemorating Christopher Columbus’s 1492 voyage across the Atlantic. But some communities observe Indigenous Peoples’ Day instead, honoring Indigenous peoples, cultures, and histories. The differing commemorations raise an important question: Who gets to decide which parts of history we celebrate, and whose experiences are left out?

The debate over whether to call it Columbus Day or Indigenous Peoples’ Day is about more than a holiday. It reveals how language influences our understanding of history and collective memory, and determines whose perspectives are treated as important.

Who Discovered America?

In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west from Europe in search of a sea route to Asia. He reached islands in the Caribbean but mistakenly believed he had arrived near Asia. His voyages helped initiate centuries of European colonization across the Americas.

Yet Columbus is still commonly described as the man who “discovered America.” This familiar expression, however, reflects a distinctly European perspective (Pennock, 2024). The Americas were already home to Indigenous peoples with established communities, cultures, languages, political systems, and histories stretching back thousands of years.

The word "discovery" is contentious. To describe a place as discovered is to imply that it was previously unknown. But unknown to whom? The land was not unknown to the people who lived there. The description makes sense only when we adopt the perspective of the arriving Europeans. This is an example of how language can reinforce a particular worldview. A familiar phrase can make one group's experience seem universal, while rendering another group's existence almost invisible.

The Power of a Name

Language does more than describe the world. It also reflects the assumptions through which we interpret it. When Columbus encountered Indigenous peoples, he thought he had reached the East Indies. This misunderstanding contributed to the use of the term "Indian" for Indigenous peoples of the Americas (Stollznow, 2020). The label originated in European geographical error rather than in the names these diverse peoples used for themselves.

Today, the appropriate terminology varies. Some people identify as American Indian, others as Native American or Indigenous, while many prefer the name of their specific nation or community. For example, Cherokee and Navajo people belong to distinct Indigenous nations, each with its own history, culture, and identity. Preferences vary, and no single term suits everyone. These differences are important because names carry histories. A label imposed by outsiders can flatten distinct identities into a single category, obscuring cultural and linguistic diversity. Using the names people choose for themselves can be a way of recognizing their agency and individuality.

article continues after advertisement

The same principle applies to the language we use when discussing historical events. Words such as settlement, colonization, invasion, and discovery can frame the same history in very different ways. Each directs attention toward certain experiences and away from others.

How Holidays Shape Collective Memory

Holidays are not simply days off work or school. They are cultural rituals that help societies decide what deserves to be remembered and celebrated. When a nation commemorates a historical figure, it sends a message about the values that figure represents. For generations, Columbus Day celebrations have often emphasized exploration, courage, and European achievement. Less attention has traditionally been given to the consequences of colonization for Indigenous communities, including dispossession, violence, and cultural disruption.

This selective remembrance is not necessarily the result of a deliberate conspiracy to conceal history. Collective memory is shaped by education, tradition, public ceremonies, political decisions, and the stories repeated across generations. Once a particular narrative becomes familiar, it can feel natural, inevitable, and even beyond question.

Changing a holiday's name can challenge that familiarity. Indigenous Peoples’ Day shifts the emphasis from celebrating a European explorer to recognizing the histories, cultures, and continuing presence of Indigenous peoples. The change does not erase Columbus from history. Instead, it invites us to reconsider which aspects of history deserve public recognition and why.

article continues after advertisement

A Debate Beyond the United States

Similar debates occur in other countries with colonial histories. In Australia, January 26 is known as "Australia Day," marking the anniversary of the arrival of the First Fleet in Sydney Harbour in 1788, an event associated with the establishment of British colonization. For many Indigenous Australians, the date represents the beginning of dispossession and profound cultural disruption. Some refer to it as Invasion Day or Survival Day, while others advocate for alternative commemorations that recognize Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and their histories (Selvanathan et al., 2023).

The competing names reveal how a national celebration can mean very different things to different communities. What one group remembers as the beginning of a nation, another may remember as the beginning of an enduring injustice. Recognizing these competing perspectives does not require us to abandon history or agree on every interpretation of the past. It requires us to acknowledge that historical narratives are constructed from particular viewpoints and that those viewpoints can exclude important experiences.

Why Words Matter

Language can preserve inherited assumptions, but it can also help us to question them. The words we use influence what we notice, which stories we remember, and whose experiences we consider worthy of recognition.

Indigenous Peoples’ Day offers an opportunity to look beyond familiar historical narratives and ask whose voices have been missing. It also reminds us that Indigenous peoples are not merely subjects of history. They are living communities with distinct identities, cultures, languages, and continuing contributions to society.

Changing the name of a holiday cannot undo the consequences of colonization. But reconsidering the language through which we remember the past can be a meaningful step toward a more inclusive understanding of history.

item.title: Loneliness and the Evolution of Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

Loneliness and the Evolution of Sleep

Sleep has changed, and research now shows a connection between it and loneliness.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Human sleep has evolved from being more communal to solitary in nature.
  • Meta-analyses have found a correlation between loneliness and sleep difficulties.
  • Sleep may be considered among the interventions for loneliness.
Research has shown a link between sleep and loneliness.
Source: Timur Weber/Pexels

A 2025 report by the World Health Organization defined loneliness as “a negative, subjective emotional state resulting from a discrepancy between one’s desired and actual experiences of connection."

Yet a definition doesn’t necessarily help with making sense of it, as Nobel (2023) noted. He viewed loneliness as a “natural biological signal,” akin to thirst or hunger or a flashing light on a mental dashboard signaling a problem.

The sleep light may be simultaneously blinking. In a meta-analysis of 27 articles, Griffin et al. (2020) found an association between loneliness and sleep disturbance, defined as “insomnia symptoms and subjective sleep quality.”

Another meta-analysis of 84 articles found a significant medium correlation between loneliness and sleep difficulties as well as loneliness and certain sleep complaints, such as poor sleep efficiency and loneliness (Hom et al., 2020). In their review of the literature, the authors discussed the idea that poor sleep may be attributed to hypervigilance to social threats in people feeling lonely. “This hypervigilance, in turn, may result in poor sleep quality and restless sleep because the brain remains vigilant even when an individual is asleep,” they added.

This notion is conceivable, given that human sleep has evolved from its start as a communal venture. Samson (2026) related that, until the mid-nineteenth century, it was normal for sleepers to share beds with others, including friends, family, and even strangers.

“From an evolutionary perspective, solitary sleep is unusual because sleep likely evolved within a social safety net,” he shared via email. “When that social context is absent or uncertain, the sleeping brain may remain more vigilant, making loneliness and poor sleep mutually reinforcing.”

Previous research by Simon and Walker (2018) examined if sleep deficit related to loneliness. In the first part of the study, the researchers studied 18 healthy adults who, in subsequent evenings, got either good and bad sleep. Through a social distancing task, the participants then indicated how close they wanted others to get to them. A brain scan of the participants followed, during which they viewed videos of people and objects approaching the camera. After that, participants were recorded answering additional questions.

article continues after advertisement

In the second part of the study, 138 participants kept track of their sleep—specifically their sleep quality—for two nights along with their daytime feelings. In the third part, Simon and Walker asked another 1033 people to view the recorded interviews from the initial segment of the study and rate the participants on behavior and appearance when both well rested and sleep-deprived.

The results were intriguing: When participants got insufficient sleep, they wanted to keep more of a distance from other people. When sleep quality worsened, loneliness was experienced the next day. Finally, the judges in the third part perceived that sleep-deprived participants were lonelier and would be less desirable to have contact with. On top of that, the judges themselves felt lonelier after viewing the videos.

Simon and Walker summarized two key findings from their study: a) the state of sleep loss should be seen as “a social repellent” and b) the asocial effects of sleep deprivation can spread even through brief interactions.

Their findings, according to Samson, are significant. “They suggest sleep loss does not simply make people feel worse internally,” he said. “It may also change social behavior in ways that push others away, creating a feedback loop between poor sleep and loneliness.”

In his view, loneliness interventions can be aided by sleep considerations, not as a cure-all, he added, “but as a modifiable physiological context that shapes vigilance, mood, and willingness to seek connection.”

The connection between slumber and loneliness isn’t one that naturally comes to mind. It is one, however, to sleep on.

item.title: What Rideshare Drivers Taught Me About Being Heard
item.description:
Empathy

What Rideshare Drivers Taught Me About Being Heard

Everyone needs an empathic witness.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness affects approximately one in six people worldwide.
  • An empathic witness is someone who listens with care without rushing to judge or fix a problem.
  • When someone shares a struggle many of us feel an immediate urge to help solve it.

I credit my second-grade teacher for giving me my first vivid memory of being listened to.

After an injustice on the playground Mrs. Bennett pulled me aside, looked at me with compassion, and said, "Tell me everything that happened. Slowly."

She let me ramble on for what felt like an hour, although it was probably 15 or 20 minutes.

Today I could not tell you what happened on the playground. I don’t recall if the kids involved were reprimanded. What I remember feeling is that something had been righted after Mrs. Bennett's intervention.

She seemed to do nothing and everything at the same time.

She listened.

She extended empathy.

She served as my empathic witness.

My intense emotions settled. I felt heard, supported, and less alone.

An empathic witness is someone who listens with care and makes room for another person’s experience, without rushing to judge or fix the problem. The presence of an empathic witness communicates what happened to you matters and I am willing to hear about it.

Years later, as a mom, therapist, and human being navigating a stressful world I observe the power of being an empathic witness repeatedly, in the most unlikely places—including the backseat of an Uber car.

I occasionally travel for work, and I have taken enough Uber rides to confidently say: Everybody needs an empathic witness, including the person taking us to our next destination.

The rides often begin in the same way. I get in the car and ask, "How are you today?"

I don't announce that I'm a therapist. I just ask with sincere interest and nine times out of ten, they tell me how they're doing.

On a recent Uber ride in Miami, a driver shared the challenges he was facing in a custody battle for his child. I listened, occasionally offering a few words of compassion.

When the 45-minute ride was over, he said, "Thank you. I haven't said that to anyone."

He sounded relieved.

I had no way to resolve his custody battle. But I could offer my attention while he put words to something painful.

In moments like these, listening can offer three important gifts:

  1. A sense of being seen. When someone takes our experience seriously, it can help us feel that our feelings and concerns matter.
  2. Relief from carrying an emotional burden alone. The circumstances may remain difficult but sharing them can make you feel emotionally lighter.
  3. Space for clear thinking. Speaking out loud can help us organize our thoughts in real time. In some instances, this can lead to clarity around the next steps.
article continues after advertisement

These small moments of connection matter within a much larger picture. In its 2025 report, the World Health Organization’s Commission on Social Connection reported that loneliness affects approximately one in six people worldwide and highlighted the importance of social connection for health and well-being.

This statistic does not tell us how many people lack an empathic witness. It does remind us how widespread the need is for meaningful connection is.

An ordinary conversation cannot replace therapy when professional care is needed, yet everyone deserves opportunities to feel heard.

On a business trip to San Diego, I had an unforgettable Uber ride, with a woman who regretted moving to a city where she was struggling financially.

Again, I said very little. Here and there I offered a comforting response: “That must have been hard,” or “That makes sense to me.”

At the end of the ride, she abruptly announced, "I know what I need to do. I have to go back home. This is not working."

I could not know whether returning home would ultimately be the right decision for her. What struck me was that she had reached her own conclusion while telling her story.

There was no magic involved. As she spoke she seemed to hear her own thoughts.

When someone shares a struggle many of us feel an immediate urge to help solve it. We reach for advice as a reflex. I have done this myself and truly meant no harm. The gesture came from a loving place. But in over 25 years as a therapist, I have learned that jumping in and trying to solve a problem while a person is still discovering what they need to do or say can add more stress to the situation.

Being an empathic witness asks us to slow down. If you are not sure what to say, you can ask: “Would you like me to listen or would it be helpful to think through some options together.”

Decades ago, Mrs. Bennett could never have known that I would remember her kindness years later. None of us know how long someone will remember that we made room for their story. These moments heal lives.

article continues after advertisement

When and where you have the emotional capacity to do so, offering yourself as an empathic witness is a gift that keeps giving toward a more compassionate world.

item.title: Who Would You Be if You Had Nothing to Prove?
item.description:
Identity

Who Would You Be if You Had Nothing to Prove?

Childhood labels shape your identity and drive your ambition

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Achievement can be driven by a desire to disprove old criticisms.
  • Negative feedback feels more believable than praise.
  • Questioning old beliefs can help us pursue new interests without tying our worth to success.
  • Examining the stories we tell ourselves can reveal whether we are living authentically or seeking validation.
geralt-wisdom
Source: Pixabay/Gerd Altmann

I want to ask you four questions I wish someone had asked them of me earlier. They might change the way you see yourself.

1. Who benefits from the way you think about yourself?

When I started first grade, I missed a lot of school because of a leg injury. I missed the basics of math, and I don't know why my elementary school teacher treated me the way she did. But whenever I struggled with a problem, she called me stupid. Eventually, I stopped doing my homework. I played with my friends instead of studying. I had accepted the idea that I wasn't smart.

When a child repeatedly hears that they are incapable, they may eventually stop questioning the message and start treating it as a fact. As I grew older, I became an honor student, received scholarships, and eventually completed my degrees in dentistry and beyond. I worked hard, and I can't deny that I'm proud of what I accomplished. But sometimes I wonder: Why was I so driven to pursue my goals? Was it because I genuinely wanted them, or was I trying to prove someone wrong? Perhaps it was both. The desire to prove someone wrong can push us toward real accomplishments, but that doesn't mean we're free from the belief that made us feel we had something to prove.

2. Who would you be without this story about yourself?

I received offers from modeling agencies. I was also encouraged to consider singing. It might sound funny, but there were people who thought my voice was workable. Of course, I refused all those offers because I was so desperate and determined to achieve all my educational goals. I thought my voice was ugly. I also thought modeling and singing weren't serious professions compared with education. I had already decided what I could and couldn't be. I chose to focus on my education.

I don't want to rewrite my past, but I wonder what else I might have explored if I hadn't been so afraid of discovering that I wasn't good at something. Would I have played the piano, or became an actress? Perhaps I would have tried these things and discovered I didn't enjoy them. That would have been fine, too, but I never even considered those possibilities.

We become so familiar with the person we believe ourselves to be that we stop questioning the limits we've placed on ourselves. If you believe you're difficult to love, perhaps you settle for relationships that confirm that belief. If you think you're not talented, perhaps you never try the thing that excites you. You might eventually forget that these were choices made under the influence of fear. Gradually, you form an "illusory" identity, until you begin to believe that's simply who you are.

article continues after advertisement

Who would you be without this story? We don’t have to be perfect or successful, or always happy. We just need to stop living in conflict with who we really are. Let your real self out.

3. When did you decide this was true?

I remember trying to solve math problems on my fingers under the desk. One day, my teacher noticed and called attention to it in front of the class. I can't say that this was the exact moment I decided I was stupid. But I remember the embarrassment, and I can see how an experience like that might have reinforced what I had already been told. A six-year-old doesn't think, "I missed lessons because I was injured, and I need more time to catch up." They're more likely to think, "There must be something wrong with me."

I grew up hearing negative messages in more than one place. I can't know exactly how each experience shaped me, but I can recognize how difficult it would be for a child to develop a secure sense of self in that environment. Years later, at university, my biochemistry professor praised me in front of my classmates. She described me as intelligent, passionate, and dedicated. Instead of enjoying her words, I felt uncomfortable. I didn't quite believe they described who I was.

The contrast is that someone could tell me I was stupid, and I would carry those words for years. Someone else could praise me, supported by my work, and I would struggle to accept it.

Have you ever noticed something similar in yourself? We often give criticism more weight than compliments.

4. What would happen if this changed?

When an article of mine gets rejected, my instinct is to work harder. I don't want to give up. I want to improve and try again. Persistence can be a good thing. Rejection is part of writing, and I don't want to lose my determination. But I also notice that I struggle to feel good about myself when I'm not productive. Resting can make me feel guilty, as though I should always be doing something useful.

What would happen if I no longer felt that I had to earn my worth through achievement? I think I would enjoy my life more. I might dance. I might learn to play the piano. I might start a podcast or pursue something creative simply because I want to see where it takes me. I wouldn't need every new interest to become a career, prove my intelligence, or make me more impressive to other people. That sounds like a small change, but to me it is a big deal: the freedom to do things without turning them into a test of who I am. I am still learning how to do that.

article continues after advertisement

The last question for you is: How much of your life are you choosing, and how much are you spending trying to prove something?

You might discover that the story you tell yourself began with a parent, a teacher, a partner, or a moment when you felt ashamed. You might discover that some parts of that story still reflect your experience, while others no longer fit. You don't have to blame anyone, dismiss your past, or abandon your ambitions to examine it. You only have to become curious about whether the story is still serving you.

I am still asking myself these questions. I don't yet know exactly who I would be if I stopped trying to prove that I was intelligent, capable, and worthy, but I want to find out.

Who would you be if you no longer had anything to prove?

item.title: Can I Just Have a Pill to Help Me Sleep?
item.description:
Sleep

Can I Just Have a Pill to Help Me Sleep?

Insomnia can be a warning sign of an underlying medical problem.

Posted October 12, 2026

Key points
  • Insomnia is a nonspecific symptom and not a diagnosis.
  • Clarifying the underlying causes of insomnia is essential for effective treatment.
  • Lifestyle habits that cause insomnia can worsen physical and mental health.

Sleep is essential for maintaining emotional and physical health. Insomnia often occurs as an indicator of an underlying problem. When it is not the result of a medical condition or related to lifestyle habits, insomnia can lead to significant medical problems.

Insomnia is a symptom, not a syndrome

A symptom is a subjective perception that a person notices regarding a specific bodily sensation or experience. Symptoms are often nonspecific and common examples include headaches, itchiness, fatigue, pain and nausea. Symptoms can serve as warning signs of an underlying disease, but are not a diagnosis in and of themselves. For example, headaches can be caused by migraines, caffeine withdrawal, alcohol hangovers, hormonal shifts or a bleed in the brain.

A syndrome refers to a condition in which multiple symptoms and objective findings exist together. For example, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) can be diagnosed when multiple signs and symptoms related to gastrointestinal dysfunction occur together. Cushing syndrome occurs when certain bodily changes result from abnormally high levels of cortisol.

If a patient consulted with an orthopedic surgeon for knee pain the surgeon would not simply recommend surgery without an assessment of what was causing the problem. That is because knee pain is a nonspecific symptom that can be related to multiple underlying medical issues. Maybe there is an infection that requires antibiotics. Perhaps the pain is related to inflammation from an autoimmune illness such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. Or maybe there is a torn ligament that needs surgical repair. The point is that the treatment for the knee pain is dependent upon what has caused it. The same is true for insomnia.

Insomnia is often a catalyst for seeking medical treatment

Although insomnia is a symptom, it is frequently conceptualized as a syndrome or diagnosis. Too often patients are simply prescribed sleeping pills without a thorough exploration of the context in which the insomnia occurs. Underlying causes of insomnia are often glossed over or are not addressed at all. Without addressing and treating the causes of insomnia, underlying medical conditions can become worse. It can also increase the risk of chronic use of sleeping pills or addiction.

Insomnia is one of the most common reasons that patients seek out psychiatric treatment. It often causes significant distress and quickly leads to spiraling anxiety about not sleeping, which can worsen the cycle of sleep disruption. It can make people feel desperate for sleeping pills.

Insomnia can worsen physical and emotional health

Poor sleep leaves people exhausted, irritable, and less focused. Chronic insomnia increases the risk of medical problems including hypertension, cardiovascular disease, weight issues, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, and colorectal cancer (Medic et al, 2017). There is a relationship between poor sleep and risk of cancer. Melatonin, a hormone involved in regulating circadian rhythm, has a role in DNA repair and inhibition of tumor growth (Medic et al, 2027). The use of electronic devices such as iPhones, televisions, and computers before going to sleep inhibits the natural production of melatonin. Disrupted sleep can affect the immune system and may lead to worsening of inflammatory bowel disease as well as irritable bowel syndrome and gastroesophageal reflux disease (Medic et al, 2017).

article continues after advertisement

In 2020, 6.3% of adults in the U.S. took daily sleep pills in the previous 30 days with an additional 2.1% using them most days and 10% using them sometimes (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2023). Risks associated with the use of sleeping pills include cognitive problems, impaired driving, and addiction.

Common causes of disrupted sleep

Here are some questions that can help determine the nature and causes of insomnia, therefore leading to the best chances of effective treatment.

  • Is the sleep disturbance new or has it been chronic? How long has it been going on?
  • How long does it take to fall asleep or fall back asleep?
  • How many hours do you sleep per night?
  • Is it trouble falling asleep, waking during the night, or awakening extra early in the morning for the day?
  • Are substances such as caffeine, alcohol, or cannabis affecting sleep?
  • Is it related to medications such as prednisone, Adderall, or over-the-counter cold medicines?
  • Is your sleep schedule inconsistent with going to sleep at different times, frequent travel with jet lag, or changing work shifts?
  • Is ambient noise, warm temperature, or a pet waking you?
  • Do you feel anxious or conflicted leading to obsessing at night?
  • Do you have a history of depression or bipolar disorder? Insomnia is often an early sign of an episode.
  • Is pain or restless legs keeping you awake?
  • Is there an underlying sleep disorder present such as obstructive sleep apnea or narcolepsy?
  • Is sleep hygiene problematic such as using screens within an hour of going to sleep or napping late in the day?

Conclusion

Determining the cause of insomnia allows for more effective treatment. Insomnia can not only result from medical problems or lifestyle issues, but it can also lead to a worsening of physical health.

If you suffer from insomnia, it is critical to examine the whole picture and not just put a bandage on it. Sleeping pills can be part of the treatment but for true health and wellness, try to elucidate the syndrome and not only treat the symptom.
